meta.blurb: The most powerful man in the Roman world writes to himself before dawn: you could leave this life at any moment, so act well now. Marcus Aurelius wrote these notes for himself, and they read like honest advice from a friend.
meta.bible: Marcus Aurelius: Roman emperor from the year 161 until his death in 180, a follower of Stoicism, who wrote a private notebook in Greek. Meditations: the modern title of that notebook, which is divided into twelve books; the Greek title found in manuscripts means To Himself. Stoicism: the ancient school of thought that teaches calm, self-control and duty, and that separates what is up to us from what is not. Rome and Roman: the empire he ruled. Danube: the river frontier where he fought long wars and wrote parts of the notebook. Rusticus: his teacher, who lent him the teachings of Epictetus. Epictetus: a former slave who became a famous Stoic teacher. Antoninus Pius: the emperor who adopted Marcus and ruled before him. Vespasian: an earlier emperor, about a century before Marcus. Caesar: the title of the emperors. Commodus: his son and successor. Vindobona and Sirmium: the two places where ancient writers say he may have died. Book numbers are given as the first book, the second book and so on. Voice and tone: calm, clear, respectful and reflective. Every idea is attributed to Marcus or to the Stoics. Never invent a quotation, and where something is uncertain, say so. Only the ideas are retold, in new words, with no long quotation. Names used in the retelling: Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Pius, Lucius Verus, Verus, Faustina, Lucilla, Verissimus, Commodus, Marcomanni, Quadi, Sarmatians, Danube, Gran, Carnuntum, Parthia, Cappadocia, Zeno, Athens, Epictetus, Rusticus, Apollonius, Sextus, Alexander, Fronto, Catulus, Severus, Maximus, Diognetus, Hippocrates, Pompey, Caesar, Augustus, Trajan, Vespasian, Diogenes, Heraclitus, Socrates, Plato, Avidius Cassius, Galen, Arethas, Xylander, Zurich, Casaubon, Frederick, Prussia, Greek, Rome, Roman, Senate, Stoic, Stoics, Stoicism, Spain, Cyprus, Arrian, Greece, Nicopolis, Cornelius, Fronto, Pompeii, Herculaneum, Vesuvius, Republic, Avidius, Faustinopolis, Constantine, Christian, Christians, Egyptian, Forum, Middle Ages, Matthew Arnold, Meric, London. Fixed facts of the retelling: Marcus was born in 121, adopted by Antoninus Pius in 138, married Faustina in 145, became emperor in 161 with Lucius Verus, who died in 169; a plague began about 165; he lived mostly on the Danube front from 169; Avidius Cassius rose in revolt in 175; Faustina died in 175; Commodus became joint emperor in 177; Marcus died in March 180. The first printed edition appeared in Zurich in 1559 and the first English translation in 1634. Ideas from Epictetus are credited to him and not to Marcus.

beats.scene: A Roman emperor in a plain tunic writes at a wooden desk
beats.summary: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor and Stoic, wrote a private notebook about how to live well.

beats.scene: An emperor writes by lamplight in a tent at a frontier camp
beats.summary: The notes are in Greek, fill twelve books, and were written for himself.

beats.scene: A closed notebook rests on a camp table beside an unlit lamp
beats.summary: The notebook had no audience: its Greek title means To Himself, and the name Meditations came long afterwards.

beats.scene: A small boy walks with his grandfather through a sunlit Roman garden
beats.summary: Marcus was born in Rome in 121, lost his father when very young, and was raised by his grandfather.

beats.scene: A grey-bearded emperor smiles down at a serious boy in a marble hall
beats.summary: Ancient writers say that Emperor Hadrian noticed the earnest boy and nicknamed him Verissimus, the most truthful.

beats.scene: A teenage boy in a white toga stands before an elderly emperor
beats.summary: In 138 Hadrian arranged that Antoninus Pius would rule after him and would adopt Marcus as his son.

beats.scene: Two men work at a long table covered with papers and scrolls
beats.summary: For twenty-three years Marcus worked beside Antoninus Pius and learned how to rule, and he married the emperor's daughter Faustina.

beats.scene: Two men in purple robes stand side by side on marble steps
beats.summary: When Pius died in 161, Marcus insisted on sharing power with his adopted brother Lucius Verus, so Rome had two emperors.

beats.scene: A cart rolls down an empty Roman street past closed shutters
beats.summary: Around 165 soldiers coming home from the war in the east spread a plague, and very many people died.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers march beside a frozen river under heavy grey skies
beats.summary: Long wars on the Danube frontier filled much of the rest of his reign, and some of the notebook was written in those camps.

beats.scene: Philosophers talk beneath a painted porch of columns in old Athens
beats.summary: The Stoic school began in Athens around 300 BC with a teacher named Zeno, who taught under a painted porch, a stoa.

beats.scene: A man looks at a stormy sea from a calm sheltered porch
beats.summary: The Stoic idea that some things are up to us and others are not.

beats.scene: Four stone columns stand in a row, each topped with a different carving
beats.summary: Stoics named four great virtues: wisdom, justice, courage and self-control.

beats.scene: A man walks across a quiet field at dawn, looking up at the sky
beats.summary: Stoics taught that to live well is to use reason and to live in harmony with nature.

beats.scene: A lame teacher speaks to a small group of students in a plain room
beats.summary: Epictetus, who was born a slave, became a famous teacher, and Marcus later read his lessons.

beats.scene: People of many nations walk together through one great city gate
beats.summary: Stoics believed that the whole world is one city and that every person is a fellow citizen.

beats.scene: Coins, a golden crown and a cup of water on a table
beats.summary: Stoics said that wealth, fame and health matter less than character, because only our choices make us good or bad.

beats.scene: A man pins a small note above his desk beside a lamp
beats.summary: Stoics practised mental exercises every day, and Marcus's notebook is one of them.

beats.scene: An emperor looks into a polished bronze mirror, unsmiling
beats.summary: Marcus often speaks to himself as you, like a student scolding himself rather than a teacher lecturing others.

beats.scene: Twelve scrolls are stacked in a row on a wooden shelf
beats.summary: The twelve books are notes added over the years, not an argument in order, so this retelling takes them one at a time.

beats.scene: An emperor writes a long list of names on a scroll in camp
beats.summary: Book one begins as a list of thanks, naming the people who shaped Marcus and what he learned from each.

beats.scene: An elderly Roman in a toga sits calmly beside a small boy
beats.summary: From his grandfather Verus he learned good character and a calm temper.

beats.scene: A boy looks up at a stone portrait of his father on a shelf
beats.summary: From his father, whom he knew only by memory and reputation, he took modesty and manliness.

beats.scene: A woman in a plain dress gives coins to a beggar at a gate
beats.summary: From his mother Lucilla he learned respect for the gods, generosity and a simple way of living.

beats.scene: Two teachers instruct a boy at a table in a quiet house
beats.summary: His great-grandfather taught him that good teachers at home are worth paying for, whatever they cost.

beats.scene: A boy sleeps on a plain wooden bed covered with a rough animal skin
beats.summary: His tutor taught him not to waste time on trifles, and he trained himself to sleep on a hard bed.

beats.scene: A teacher hands a worn scroll to a young student
beats.summary: Book one: his teacher Rusticus lends him the teachings of Epictetus.

beats.scene: A student reads slowly, one finger moving under each line of a scroll
beats.summary: Rusticus also taught him to train his character, to write plain letters and to read carefully instead of skimming.

beats.scene: A man lies calmly in bed while worried friends stand around him
beats.summary: Apollonius showed him a life that was both firm and gentle, calm even in sharp pain.

beats.scene: A father and sons share a long dinner table with relatives
beats.summary: From Sextus he learned kindness and a household run with fatherly love.

beats.scene: A teacher gently says a word aloud while a student smiles
beats.summary: The grammarian Alexander taught him to correct a mistake kindly, by simply using the right word.

beats.scene: A famous teacher of speech stands before a crowded lecture room
beats.summary: Fronto, a famous teacher of speech, helped him see the envy and pretence that power breeds.

beats.scene: A man puts down his pen to listen to a visitor at the door
beats.summary: Alexander the Platonist taught him never to excuse himself from helping by saying he was too busy.

beats.scene: Two friends sit talking quietly after an argument
beats.summary: Catulus taught him to listen to a friend's complaint even when it seemed unfair.

beats.scene: A bronze statue of a famous Roman stands in a shaded courtyard
beats.summary: Severus showed him love of family, truth and justice, and the idea of a free state with equal rights.

beats.scene: A man works on through an illness, smiling at his friends
beats.summary: Maximus gave him an example of self-control and cheerfulness, even in sickness.

beats.scene: An older emperor in plain clothes listens patiently to advisers
beats.summary: Book one: Marcus honours Antoninus Pius, the emperor who adopted him.

beats.scene: A ruler decides a question at a desk of plain wood
beats.summary: From Pius he learned to decide after careful thought, to stay firm, and not to be vain about honours.

beats.scene: An emperor shares a simple dinner with friends in a plain room
beats.summary: Pius lived simply, dined at home with friends and never forced them to follow him on every journey.

beats.scene: A man gazes at a starry sky from a camp beside a river
beats.summary: Book one ends with thanks to the gods for good family, teachers, a brother, a wife and children, and is marked as written among the Quadi on the Gran.

beats.scene: A man steps out of his front door into a busy street at sunrise
beats.summary: Book two: begin each day expecting to meet difficult people.

beats.scene: A calm man stands untouched while an angry crowd shouts around him
beats.summary: Marcus tells himself that other people's bad behaviour cannot spoil his character unless he lets it.

beats.scene: Two men carry a heavy beam together across a Roman yard
beats.summary: Book two: people are made to work together like hands and feet.

beats.scene: A man pushes a pile of books aside and lifts his head
beats.summary: He reminds himself that he is only flesh, a little breath and a ruling mind, and tells himself to put his books down.

beats.scene: An older man looks at a long row of unfinished tasks on a table
beats.summary: Marcus reminds himself how long he has been putting things off and how many chances he has not used.

beats.scene: A water clock drips slowly beside a half-written page
beats.summary: Book two: life is short and might end at any moment, so act well now.

beats.scene: A man sits alone in a tent at night with his head bowed
beats.summary: He scolds his own soul for failing to honour itself, because life is almost over.

beats.scene: A tree branch lies cut off on the ground beside its tree
beats.summary: A person who cuts himself off from other people, he says, is like a branch cut from its tree.

beats.scene: A traveller rests at a roadside inn with a dusty pack
beats.summary: Book two: life is a brief journey, and only philosophy can guide us.

beats.scene: A scroll's last line is written beside a Roman camp wall
beats.summary: Book two ends with a note that it was written at Carnuntum, a Roman camp on the Danube.

beats.scene: A white-haired man rests his hand on his forehead beside an oil lamp
beats.summary: Book three warns that life is being used up every day, and that the mind may weaken before life ends.

beats.scene: A man walks alone in thought past a gossiping crowd
beats.summary: Book three: do not waste life thinking about other people's business.

beats.scene: Three stone tombs stand in a row beside a quiet road
beats.summary: Marcus lists great men who died anyway: the doctor Hippocrates, the conqueror Alexander and the general Pompey.

beats.scene: A loaf of bread with a cracked golden crust sits on a table
beats.summary: Book three: even things that look imperfect can have their own beauty.

beats.scene: Ripe figs split open on a branch in the warm sun
beats.summary: He adds figs that split when very ripe and olives about to fall: even these have a beauty of their own.

beats.scene: A sentry waits on a high wall for the trumpet at dusk
beats.summary: He tells himself to live like a soldier at his post, ready to leave when the signal comes.

beats.scene: A man refuses a heavy bag of gold and walks on
beats.summary: Nothing is worth having, he says, if it makes you break your word, lose self-respect or hate other people.

beats.scene: A craftsman strips the carved decoration from a vase to show plain clay
beats.summary: He advises looking at each thing as it really is, describing it plainly and breaking it into its parts.

beats.scene: A carpenter bends over a bench, working in a quiet empty workshop
beats.summary: He tells himself to do each task seriously, with energy and calm, as if he might have to give back his own mind at any moment.

beats.scene: A small flame burns steadily in a glass lantern in a gale
beats.summary: A mind that does its duty, speaks the truth and accepts what it is given, he concludes, has nothing to fear from fate.

beats.scene: A crowd walks along a beach toward distant blue mountains
beats.summary: In book four Marcus notes that people long for retreats in the countryside, by the sea or in the hills.

beats.scene: A man sits quietly alone on a bench in a small walled garden
beats.summary: Book four: the best retreat is inside your own mind.

beats.scene: A man keeps a few short notes ready in a leather pouch
beats.summary: He keeps two short principles ready: things outside us cannot touch the mind, and everything we see will soon change.

beats.scene: A man calmly reads a letter that contains bad news
beats.summary: Book four: take away the opinion that you are harmed, and the harm goes too.

beats.scene: A man crosses items off a very long list with a single stroke
beats.summary: Do fewer things, he says, and you will find more peace, because most of what we say and do is not necessary.

beats.scene: A fast river carries leaves and branches past a stone bridge
beats.summary: Book four: time is a river that sweeps everything away.

beats.scene: Waves crash against a tall rocky headland that stands unmoved
beats.summary: Book four: be like a headland that the waves cannot move.

beats.scene: A fire burns brighter as a log is thrown into the flames
beats.summary: A strong mind treats obstacles as a fire treats fuel: it turns them into light.

beats.scene: A gardener waters tidy vegetable beds at sunrise
beats.summary: He tells himself that whatever suits the world suits him, and that nothing comes too early or too late.

beats.scene: A single candle burns beside a closed door at night
beats.summary: Death hangs over you, he says, so while you can, be good.

beats.scene: A quiet street of an ancient town lies under grey volcanic ash
beats.summary: Marcus thinks of whole cities that disappeared, such as Pompeii and Herculaneum, buried by the volcano Vesuvius in the year 79.

beats.scene: Crumbling stone columns stand in tall grass beneath a grey sky
beats.summary: Book four: the busy people of Vespasian's time have vanished, and so will we.

beats.scene: Two worn marble heads lie in the tall grass of an old garden
beats.summary: Even great rulers such as Augustus and Hadrian, he says, are now nobody and nowhere.

beats.scene: A stone portrait of a forgotten man stands in a dusty courtyard
beats.summary: Book four: fame after death does not last, because everyone is forgotten.

beats.scene: A row of people each point to the next one, fading into mist
beats.summary: Those who remember you will die, then those who remember them, until the memory is gone.

beats.scene: A tiny figure stands at the edge of a vast empty plain
beats.summary: He compares our share of time and matter with the whole: a short span and a tiny portion.

beats.scene: A green shoot rises from a fallen seed in a ploughed field
beats.summary: Nature loves change, he says, and what exists today is the seed of what comes next.

beats.scene: A ripe olive falls from a tree on a hillside in autumn
beats.summary: He hopes to pass through his short time as a ripe olive falls: grateful to the tree that bore it.

beats.scene: A green gemstone lies on a velvet cloth in bright sunlight
beats.summary: Beautiful things need no praise, he says: an emerald is no better or worse for being admired.

beats.scene: A man walks briskly out of a crowded square into quiet fields
beats.summary: From all these reminders Marcus draws one plain lesson: stop chasing fame and live well in the time you have.

beats.scene: A man sits up in a cold bedroom as dawn light enters
beats.summary: Book five: on a hard morning, remember that you rise to do a human being's work.

beats.scene: Ants, bees and a sparrow are busy on a garden wall at dawn
beats.summary: Marcus notes that plants, birds, ants and bees all do their own work, so a human being should not refuse his.

beats.scene: A man lies under thick blankets while the sun rises outside his window
beats.summary: Was he made to lie in warm blankets, he asks himself, and answers that people were made to act, not only to enjoy comfort.

beats.scene: A vine heavy with grapes grows quietly on a sunny wall
beats.summary: Book five: the best kind of giver is like a vine that asks for nothing.

beats.scene: A man wipes a slate clean with a damp cloth
beats.summary: It is easy, he says, to wipe away every troublesome thought and then to be at peace.

beats.scene: A cloth is dipped into a vat of deep blue dye
beats.summary: Book five: the mind is dyed by the thoughts we repeat.

beats.scene: A fallen tree blocks a mountain path and a traveller climbs over it
beats.summary: Book five: what stands in the way becomes the way.

beats.scene: A doctor writes instructions on a wax tablet beside a sick man
beats.summary: Accept what happens as you would a doctor's orders, even when they are bitter, for they serve your health.

beats.scene: A man gets up again after stumbling on a rocky path
beats.summary: When you fail, he says, do not be disgusted; return to the task, and be glad if most of what you do is truly human.

beats.scene: Two men stand close together in a crowded hall, one frowning, one smiling
beats.summary: With dry humour he asks what use anger is against a person's bad breath, since such a mouth and such a smell go together.

beats.scene: A guard stands steady on a wall in the rain
beats.summary: Book six: do your duty whether you are cold or warm.

beats.scene: A man finishes his task at dusk with a calm, steady face
beats.summary: Even dying, he says, is one of the acts of life, so do it as well as you do everything else.

beats.scene: A man turns away from an angry crowd and walks calmly down a road
beats.summary: Book six: the best revenge is not to become like the wrongdoer.

beats.scene: Two plain graves of the same size lie side by side on a hill
beats.summary: Alexander the Great and his mule driver, Marcus notes, ended up in the same place.

beats.scene: A roast meal, a glass of wine and a purple robe on a table
beats.summary: Book six: see fine things as they really are, without the glamour.

beats.scene: A man looks from a map of Rome to a globe
beats.summary: As an emperor his city is Rome, but as a human being his city is the world, and what helps both is the only good for him.

beats.scene: A purple imperial cloak hangs unworn on a plain wooden peg
beats.summary: Book six: Marcus warns himself not to be changed by power.

beats.scene: Bees crowd around a honeycomb inside a wooden hive
beats.summary: Book six: what is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee.

beats.scene: A man lifts a heavy stone with both hands, strained but steady
beats.summary: If something is humanly possible, Marcus tells himself, believe that you can do it too.

beats.scene: A man stands between a watchful garden and a scattered heap of seeds
beats.summary: Whether the world is ruled by fate, by providence or by no one, he says, he still has a mind that can be good.

beats.scene: A traveller on a hill path looks at the road behind and ahead
beats.summary: Book seven: accept what happens to you, as part of your own life.

beats.scene: A man walks from one task to the next along a busy lane
beats.summary: He finds his pleasure in passing from one helpful act to the next, with the gods in mind.

beats.scene: A green gemstone sits calmly in a stream of muddy water
beats.summary: Whatever anyone does or says, Marcus tells himself, I must be good, as an emerald must keep its colour.

beats.scene: A man digs a well in dry ground and clear water rises
beats.summary: Book seven: the fountain of goodness is inside you, if you keep digging.

beats.scene: A patient man rests in bed by a window as morning light enters
beats.summary: Book seven: pain has limits, and imagination can make it worse.

beats.scene: A wrestler and a gladiator face each other in a sandy ring
beats.summary: In the art of living, he says, be like the wrestler rather than the gladiator, who must put down his sword and may die.

beats.scene: A man gently helps a stranger who has stumbled up a hill
beats.summary: It is human, he says, to love even those who wrong us, because they are our relatives and they do not know better.

beats.scene: A lame soldier is hoisted up a wall by a comrade
beats.summary: Do not be ashamed to be helped, he says, for a soldier who cannot climb alone must be glad of a friend.

beats.scene: A man watches the sun rise over a quiet roof, calm and unhurried
beats.summary: The perfection of character, he says, is to spend each day as if it were the last, without frenzy, dullness or pretence.

beats.scene: Threads of many colours weave together on a large wooden loom
beats.summary: Book seven: all things are woven together in one order.

beats.scene: A stone tower stands strong on a hill above a quiet town
beats.summary: Book eight: a mind free of strong passions is a citadel.

beats.scene: A plain cloak hangs on a hook beside a golden imperial robe
beats.summary: He admits that he has not been seen as a philosopher, because life at court and in camp stands in the way, so he lets the wish go.

beats.scene: Three famous thinkers sit in a bare room while three conquerors ride past
beats.summary: He sets the conquerors Alexander, Caesar and Pompey beside the thinkers Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates, and prefers the thinkers.

beats.scene: A traveller steps around a thorny bush on a country road
beats.summary: Book eight: throw away the bitter cucumber and avoid the thorns, without complaint.

beats.scene: A teacher patiently shows a young learner how to do a task
beats.summary: Book eight: people exist for one another, so teach them or bear with them.

beats.scene: A man wipes dust from a window and light floods the room
beats.summary: When something outside troubles you, he says, the pain comes from your judgment, and you have the power to wipe it out.

beats.scene: A smooth bright ball rests on a plain stone table in sunlight
beats.summary: The mind is at its best, he says, when it neither stretches out toward things nor shrinks inward, like a smooth round sphere.

beats.scene: A man stops at a street corner and takes a slow breath
beats.summary: Do not picture your whole life's troubles at once, he says; ask what is hard about this moment, and bear that.

beats.scene: An old man gently holds the hand of a young traveller
beats.summary: He plays on two Greek words, part and limb: if you feel like a limb of the body of humanity, you do good for the joy of it.

beats.scene: A man in a plain tunic walks through a grand marble palace
beats.summary: He reminds himself that where life is possible, a good life is possible, even in a palace.

beats.scene: A man looks into a still pool and frowns at his own face
beats.summary: Book nine: whoever does wrong does wrong to himself.

beats.scene: A circle of different people sit around one long table, passing bread
beats.summary: Injustice goes against nature, he says, because nature made thinking beings for one another.

beats.scene: A leaf drifts down from an autumn tree onto a quiet pond
beats.summary: Book nine: death is natural, so do not despise it.

beats.scene: A mother cradles a newborn while an old man naps beside the fire
beats.summary: Death is a change of nature, like birth, and waiting for it is like waiting for a baby to be born.

beats.scene: A man leaves a crowded room quietly while the others talk on
beats.summary: He writes that only friends who share his views could make him wish to stay, and that the discord of life with others is wearying.

beats.scene: A shameless man shouts in a market while a calm man passes by
beats.summary: When shameless people offend you, he says, ask whether the world could be without them, and do not expect the impossible.

beats.scene: A scroll lies open beside a bust of a bearded philosopher
beats.summary: Do not hope for Plato's perfect Republic, he says, but be content if the smallest thing goes well.

beats.scene: A priest in a white toga stands at an altar with his head covered
beats.summary: As emperor Marcus was also Rome's chief priest, and he spoke of the gods without arguing over what they are.

beats.scene: An empty banquet hall holds dusty couches and cold lamps
beats.summary: He tours the court of Augustus in his mind, where wife, daughter, friends, doctors and priests are all gone.

beats.scene: A man walks home from a hillside cemetery at sunset with open hands
beats.summary: Thinking about death does not make Marcus bitter; it makes him gentle, patient and attentive to the day.

beats.scene: Tiny villages, rivers and fields lie below a high mountain ridge
beats.summary: Book nine: see life from above, and worries shrink to their true size.

beats.scene: A tiny dot of earth hangs in a wide field of stars
beats.summary: He reminds himself how small the earth is, a point in the universe, and how much smaller fame is.

beats.scene: An old man watches the same hills in the same light each morning
beats.summary: Everything is familiar, he says, and whoever has seen the present has seen all that ever was or will be.

beats.scene: Three groups of travellers in different clothes walk the same road
beats.summary: The same things happen again and again in new costumes, and the world has seen all these plays before.

beats.scene: A man stands steady on a ship's deck as waves rise around it
beats.summary: Wipe away your imaginings, he says, check your impulses, quiet your wants and keep the ruling mind in your own hands.

beats.scene: A man's outline is drawn with three glowing parts, body, breath and mind
beats.summary: He divides a person into body, breath of life and mind, and says only the mind is truly our own.

beats.scene: A spider sits proudly on a web holding a fly
beats.summary: He jokes that a spider is proud of catching a fly, a man of catching a hare, and a general of capturing a tribe.

beats.scene: Ants carry loads, mice scatter and puppets dance on strings
beats.summary: The shows of the court and the arena look to a wise eye like puppets on strings and ants carrying crumbs.

beats.scene: A scale weighs a small bag of seeds against a large pile of straw
beats.summary: Each person is worth as much as the things he cares about, Marcus says, so choose what to care for.

beats.scene: A crowded bathhouse with steaming pools and wet tiles
beats.summary: He compares ordinary life to a visit to the baths, with its oil, sweat, dirt and greasy water.

beats.scene: A man in plain clothes helps a neighbour carry water
beats.summary: Book ten: do not argue about what a good person is; be one.

beats.scene: A man walks alone on a mountain track overlooking a city
beats.summary: Live as if on a mountain, he says: it does not matter where you live, as long as you live as a citizen of the world.

beats.scene: Surgeon's tools lie open on a clean white cloth
beats.summary: As a doctor keeps instruments ready, keep your principles ready, so you can act well at a moment's notice.

beats.scene: A man bows to greet a neighbour with a basket at his feet
beats.summary: A person's true joy is to do human things: be kind, ignore bodily urges, test first impressions and study nature.

beats.scene: A man pauses at a doorway and weighs a decision
beats.summary: He often tests an action by asking whether it is needed and whether it serves the people around him.

beats.scene: A balance scale holds a gold coin and an olive
beats.summary: Wealth and poverty, honour and shame, health and sickness come to good and bad people alike, so they cannot be what makes a life good.

beats.scene: A man writes at a desk and looks up at the sky
beats.summary: In book ten he asks his own soul whether it will ever be simple, honest, kind and content with the present.

beats.scene: Autumn leaves blow down a street full of walking people
beats.summary: He recalls an old poet's line that people are like leaves, scattered by the wind, and that this includes those who praise us.

beats.scene: A man stands at a gate looking calmly down a long road
beats.summary: He tells himself not to fear the future, for he will meet it with the same reason he has now.

beats.scene: A man leans forward to hear a speaker, giving him his whole attention
beats.summary: He tells himself to listen with his whole mind and to enter into what the speaker really means.

beats.scene: A man takes a deep breath and unclenches his fists
beats.summary: Book eleven: anger and distress do more harm than the thing that caused them.

beats.scene: A man offers a cup of water to a scowling visitor
beats.summary: Book eleven: sincere kindness cannot be defeated.

beats.scene: Two men face each other at a table, one angry and one calm
beats.summary: Before judging another, he says, remember that you too have done many things wrong, and you cannot be sure the other person is wrong.

beats.scene: A tall man bends to speak softly to a shouting man
beats.summary: Gentleness and kindness are more truly human and manly than rage, he says: strength belongs to the kind, not the angry.

beats.scene: A father gently takes a boy's hand to show him how to do it

B1B2: Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire from the year 161 until his death in 180. He was a follower of Stoicism, an ancient school of thought, and he wrote down private notes about how to live well.
Marcus wrote his notes in Greek, and they fill twelve short books. Two of them say that they were written in army camps, far from Rome, and he probably never meant anyone else to read them.
The Greek title found in the oldest copies simply means To Himself, as if the book were a private letter. The name Meditations was added much later, by the people who first printed and sold it.
Marcus was born in Rome in the year 121 into a wealthy and well-known family. His father died while he was still a small child, so his grandfather helped to raise him.
Ancient writers say that Emperor Hadrian noticed the serious young Marcus and gave him a nickname. He called the boy Verissimus, which means the most truthful.
In 138 the old emperor Hadrian chose Antoninus Pius to rule after him. He also told Pius to adopt the teenage Marcus as his son.
For twenty-three years Marcus worked beside Antoninus Pius, learning how a good ruler spends his days. In 145 he married the emperor's daughter, Faustina, and they began a large family.
Antoninus Pius died in 161, and Marcus could easily have ruled alone, as the Senate expected. Instead he insisted on sharing the throne with his adoptive brother, Lucius Verus.
Around 165 soldiers returning from the war in the east brought a deadly plague with them. It spread across the empire, and very many people died.
Tribes crossed the Danube frontier, and Marcus spent years in army camps there. Some of his notebook was written in those camps, far from the comforts of Rome.
The Stoic school began in Athens around 300 BC, taught by a man named Zeno. His students met under a painted porch, which in Greek is called a stoa.

The Stoics taught that some things are up to us, such as our thoughts and our choices, and others are not. Wealth, fame, the weather and other people's opinions all belong to the second group, and Marcus reminds himself of this again and again.
The Stoics named four great virtues, which were wisdom, justice, courage and self-control. A person who has all four, they believed, is a good person whatever else happens in life.
Stoics taught that human beings are the animals that can reason. To live well, they said, is to use that reason and to live in harmony with nature.
Epictetus was born a slave, and later he became free and taught philosophy in Greece. His student Arrian wrote down his lessons, and Marcus read them.
The Stoics believed that the whole world is one city, shared by gods and human beings. Every person, they said, is a fellow citizen, whatever country he comes from.
The Stoics said that wealth, fame and health matter less than character. Only our own choices, they taught, can make us truly good or bad.
For the Stoics, philosophy was a daily exercise, like training for an athlete. Marcus's notebook is one such exercise, made of short reminders written to keep his mind steady.
In the notebook Marcus often speaks to himself as if he were a stubborn pupil. He scolds, encourages and sometimes gives himself orders, but he never lectures the world.
The twelve books are notes added over many years, not one argument from start to finish. This retelling takes them one by one, in order, with a few steps outside to meet the man.
The first book is not a lesson but a list of thanks. Marcus names the people who shaped him and says what he learned from each of them.
Marcus thanks his grandfather Verus for his good character and his calm temper. Both, he implies, are things a child learns by watching an adult he loves.
Marcus barely knew his father, who died when he was small. But he remembered his father's good name and took from it a sense of modesty and manliness.
From his mother Lucilla he learned respect for the gods and a generous heart. She also showed him a simple way of living, far from the habits of the rich.
His great-grandfather taught him to have good teachers at home instead of going to public schools. He also taught him that such teachers are worth any price.

A tutor taught him not to waste time on trifles, and he trained himself to sleep on a hard wooden bed. He also learned to put up with plain food and rough clothes, as Greek students of philosophy did.

Marcus thanks his teacher Rusticus for showing him that he needed to train his character, and for not letting him show off. Rusticus also lent him his own copy of the teachings of Epictetus, a former slave who became a famous Stoic teacher.
Rusticus taught Marcus that his character needed training, and he warned him against showy speeches. He also taught him to write plain letters and to read books carefully, not just quickly.
Apollonius showed him a life that was both firm and gentle. He stayed calm even in sharp pain, and he judged everything by reason alone.
From Sextus he learned kindness and the example of a household run with a father's love. Sextus was natural and never false, and he was patient with people who knew little.
The grammarian Alexander taught him not to scold people for their mistakes. Instead he would simply use the right word in his own reply, and let them hear it.
Fronto, the most famous teacher of speech in Rome, helped Marcus see the envy and pretence that power can breed. He also noticed that the great families of Rome could be cold to their own relatives.
Alexander the Platonist taught him not to say, again and again, that he was too busy. Being busy, he learned, is a poor reason to ignore the people around us.
Catulus taught him not to ignore a friend's complaint, even when it seemed unfair. He also taught him to praise his teachers sincerely and to love his own children.
Severus showed him love of family, truth and justice. He also showed him the idea of a free state in which everyone has equal rights and may speak freely.
Maximus gave him an example of self-control and cheerfulness, even in sickness. He worked without complaint, and people believed that what he said was what he meant.

Marcus remembers Antoninus Pius, the emperor before him, who had adopted him as a son. He admired his calm and his fairness, and the way he listened to advice and rarely took a quick decision just to look strong.
From Pius he learned to decide after careful thought and then to stay firm. He also learned not to be vain about honours, and to work hard at his tasks.
Pius lived a simple life and often dined at home with his friends. He never forced them to follow him on every journey, and they were free to stay at home.
Book one ends with thanks to the gods for a good family, good teachers, a brother, a wife and children. The last line says it was written among the Quadi, by the river Gran.
Begin the day by telling yourself that you will meet rude, selfish and dishonest people, Marcus wrote. They act this way, he thought, because they do not know what is truly good.
Marcus tells himself that rude people cannot harm him unless he lets them. No one, he says, can drag his character into ugliness without his consent.
We were born to work together, wrote Marcus, like feet, hands, eyes and the two rows of teeth. To act against each other, he concluded, is to act against our own nature.
Whatever I am, Marcus tells himself, it is a little flesh, a little breath and a mind that rules. So he orders himself to put down his books and stop being pulled in every direction.
Remember how long you have been putting things off, Marcus tells himself. The gods have given you many chances, and you have not used them.
You could leave life this very moment, Marcus told himself, so let that guide what you do, say and think. He did not mean this as a sad thought, but as a reason to act well today.
You are insulting yourself, my soul, he writes, and soon you will have no chance to honour yourself. Your life is almost over, and you are looking for happiness in other people's opinions.
Marcus writes that a branch cut off from its neighbour is cut off from the whole tree. In the same way, a person who turns away from other people turns away from all humanity.

Marcus wrote that a human life is only a point in time, and that the world around it is always flowing and changing. Life, he said, is like a journey through a foreign land, and soon the traveller is forgotten.
At the end of book two a note says it was written at Carnuntum. This was a large Roman camp on the Danube, near the modern city of Vienna.
Life is being used up every day, Marcus warns, and a little less of it remains. We must also ask whether our minds will stay sharp until the end.
Do not waste what is left of your life thinking about other people, Marcus wrote, unless it helps someone. Wondering what a neighbour is doing, saying or planning takes you away from your own work.

Marcus reminds himself that the doctor Hippocrates cured many sick people and then died himself. The conqueror Alexander and the general Pompey died too, though they had destroyed whole cities in war.
Marcus noticed that even things that look imperfect can have a charm of their own. The cracks in the crust of baked bread, he wrote, and the ripe figs that split open, are pleasing to see.
A fig that is very ripe splits open, he notes, and an olive that is about to fall has a beauty of its own. Neither is perfect, yet both please us because they follow their own nature.
Do each act as a Roman and a man should, Marcus tells himself. Live like a soldier at his post, ready to leave when the signal sounds.
Never value as a gain, Marcus says, anything that makes you break your word or lose your self-respect. Nothing is worth that, whether it is money, power or pleasure.
Always ask what a thing is in itself, Marcus advises, and break it into its parts. Seen plainly, many things that impress us are much smaller than they seemed.
Do each task seriously, with energy and calm, Marcus advises. Behave, he says, as if you could be asked to give back your own mind at any moment.
A mind that does its duty and tells the truth is not afraid of fate. Marcus says that such a person is content with what he is given, and he lives well.
People long for quiet places in the countryside, by the sea or in the hills, Marcus says. He says it is a very ordinary wish, and one he feels himself.
People look for quiet places in the countryside, by the sea or in the mountains, wrote Marcus. But you can retreat into your own mind at any hour, and nowhere is calmer than that.
Marcus keeps two short thoughts ready for any trouble. Things outside us cannot touch the mind, he says, and everything we see will soon change.
Take away your opinion, Marcus wrote, and the complaint “I have been harmed” disappears. Take away the complaint, and the harm itself disappears too.
Do fewer things, Marcus says, if you want to be calm. Most of what we say and do is not necessary, so we can drop it.
Time is like a river of passing events with a strong current, Marcus wrote. As soon as something comes into sight, it is swept away, and something else takes its place.
Be like a headland, Marcus told himself, a rock that sticks out into the sea. The waves crash against it again and again, but it stands firm, and the water around it grows calm.
A good fire burns whatever is thrown into it, Marcus says, and rises higher. A strong mind uses every obstacle in the same way, to grow brighter.
Whatever suits the world also suits him, Marcus writes, and nothing arrives too early or too late for him. Everything the seasons of nature bring is fruit to him, and he welcomes it all.
Do not act as if you will live ten thousand years, Marcus tells himself. Death hangs over you, so while you can, be good.
Marcus thinks of whole cities that have disappeared, such as Pompeii and Herculaneum. A volcano buried them in the year 79, and later people had to dig them up.

Think of the time of the emperor Vespasian, Marcus wrote, and you will see people marrying, trading, farming, arguing and making plans. All of that busy life has vanished, and our own life will vanish too.
Soon you will be nobody and nowhere, Marcus tells himself, just like Augustus and Hadrian. These great emperors once ruled the world, and now they are only names.

People who long to be remembered after death forget, wrote Marcus, that everyone who remembers them will soon die as well. Memory passes from one person to the next, and at last it goes out like a candle.
Those who remember you will die, Marcus says, and then those who remember them. In the end the memory goes out like a flame.
Think of all of time and all the matter in the world, Marcus says, and how small your share is. Your life is only a short moment in a very long story.
The universe loves to change things and make new ones, Marcus says. What exists now is like the seed of what will come next.
Pass through this short time in harmony with nature, Marcus says, and end it gladly. An olive falls when it is ripe, and it thanks the tree that bore it.
Whatever is beautiful is beautiful in itself, Marcus says, and praise adds nothing to it. A flower or a jewel is not made better or worse by being admired.
From all these thoughts about dust and forgetting, Marcus draws one plain lesson. Stop chasing fame, and live well in the time that you have.
When you find it hard to get out of bed, Marcus told himself, remember that you are rising to do a human being's work. Were you born to lie under the blankets and keep warm?
Plants, birds, ants, spiders and bees all do their own work, Marcus notes, and help to order the world. So why, he asks himself, should a human being refuse to do his?
It is more pleasant under the blankets, says the lazy voice inside him. But were you made only for pleasure, Marcus answers, and not for action?
Some people do a kindness and then expect a reward, Marcus wrote, and others quietly remember what they did. A third kind, he said, is like a vine that gives grapes and asks for nothing more.
How easy it is to wipe away every troublesome thought, Marcus writes, and to be completely at peace. He treats the mind like a slate that can be cleaned.
The kind of thoughts you often have, wrote Marcus, will be the kind of mind that you have. The soul is dyed by its thoughts, so we should choose them with care.
What stands in the way becomes the way, wrote Marcus, because an obstacle to action can help action forward. A problem is a chance to practise patience, courage or kindness.
We say that a doctor has ordered a walk or a cold bath, Marcus notes. In the same way, he says, nature may order an illness or a loss.
Do not be disgusted or discouraged when you fail, Marcus tells himself, but return to the task. Be content if most of what you do is truly human.
With dry humour, Marcus asks what use anger is against a person whose breath smells bad. Such a mouth and such a smell go together, he says, so why be surprised?
Let it make no difference to you whether you are cold or warm, Marcus wrote, as long as you are doing your duty. It should not matter either whether you are tired, praised or blamed.
Even dying is one of the acts of life, Marcus says, so we should do it well. A good person does not need to fear it, only to meet it calmly.
The best revenge, wrote Marcus, is not to become like the person who wronged you. If someone behaves badly, answering in the same way only doubles the harm.
Alexander the Great and his mule driver, Marcus notes, were brought to the same state by death. Either they were taken back into the same life of the world, or both were scattered into tiny pieces.
When you see fine food, Marcus wrote, tell yourself that this is the body of a dead fish or bird. Fine wine is only grape juice, and a purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with the juice of a shellfish.
As an emperor, Marcus writes, my city and country is Rome, but as a human being it is the world. Only what helps both of these cities, he says, is truly good for me.
See that you are not turned into a Caesar, Marcus warned himself, and do not be dyed with that dye. Stay simple, good, honest, serious and a friend of justice, he said.
What is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee, wrote Marcus. He believed that a person is part of a community, and that we cannot truly thrive at the cost of others.
Do not think that something is impossible just because it is hard for you, Marcus tells himself. If it is humanly possible, believe that you can do it too.
In one passage Marcus considers three possibilities: fate, kind providence, or confusion without a ruler. Whichever is true, he says, he can still try to be a good person.
Love only what happens to you, wrote Marcus, because it is woven into the thread of your life. The saying does not claim that everything is pleasant, but it asks us to meet events without complaint.
Take pleasure in one thing only, Marcus tells himself: passing from one helpful act to another. Each kind deed, with the gods in mind, is a place to rest.
An emerald, Marcus imagines, would say that whatever anyone does or says, it must be an emerald and keep its colour. So he tells himself to stay good, whatever others do.
Look within, wrote Marcus, because within is a fountain of goodness. It will keep bubbling up, he said, as long as you keep digging.

Pain is neither unbearable nor endless, wrote Marcus, if you remember its limits and do not add to it in your imagination. He does not say that pain is unreal, only that the mind can ease or worsen how it feels.
In the art of living, Marcus says, be like the wrestler and not the gladiator. A gladiator who drops his sword may be killed, but a wrestler always has his hands.
It is a mark of being human, Marcus says, to love even the people who wrong us. We can do it by remembering that they are our relatives and that they do not know any better.
Do not be ashamed to be helped, Marcus says. A soldier who cannot climb a wall alone is glad when a comrade lends a hand.
The perfection of character, Marcus says, is to spend each day as if it were your last. Do it calmly, without frenzy, without laziness and without any pretence.
All things are tied to one another, wrote Marcus, and the bond between them is sacred. Hardly anything in the world, he thought, stands completely alone.

A mind that is free from strong passions is like a citadel, wrote Marcus, because a person has nothing safer to run to. Anyone who knows this and still does not take shelter there, he said, is unhappy.
Marcus admits that he is far from looking like a philosopher, because court and camp life stand in the way. So he lets the wish go and tries only to do what is needed.

Marcus compares the conquerors Alexander, Caesar and Pompey with the thinkers Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates. The thinkers, he says, understood the world, while the conquerors were slaves to their huge plans.

If a cucumber is bitter, Marcus wrote, throw it away, and if there are thorns on the road, turn aside from them. That is enough, he said, and there is no need to ask why such things exist in the world.
People exist for the sake of one another, wrote Marcus, so either teach them or put up with them. It is a short rule for dealing with difficult people, and it avoids both anger and contempt.
If something outside troubles you, Marcus says, it is not the thing itself but your judgment of it. You have the power to wipe out that judgment at any moment.
A mind is at its best, Marcus says, when it is like a smooth round sphere. It does not stretch out toward things, and it does not shrink inward.
Do not disturb yourself by picturing your whole life at once, Marcus says. Ask what is hard about this moment, and bear that.
In Greek there are two similar words, part and limb, Marcus notes. If you think of yourself as a limb, you will love other people, because you are one body.
Where it is possible to live, Marcus reasons, it is possible to live well. Since life is possible in a palace, a good life is possible there too.
He who does wrong does wrong to himself, wrote Marcus, because he makes himself a worse person. A person who lies or cheats, he thought, damages his own character before he damages anyone else's.
Acting unjustly goes against nature, Marcus says, because nature made thinking beings for one another. They should help each other, not harm each other.

Do not despise death, wrote Marcus, but welcome it, because it too is one of the things that nature wills. He compared it to the natural stages of life, such as growing up, growing old and growing teeth.
Marcus compares death to birth, for both are changes made by nature. A person who waits calmly for a child to be born, he says, can wait calmly for his own end.
Only one thing could make me want to stay, Marcus writes: friends who think as I do. But he sees how much discord there is in life with other people.
When shameless people offend you, Marcus says, ask whether the world could be without them. It could not, so do not ask for something impossible.

Do not hope for Plato's perfect Republic, Marcus tells himself, because that is asking for too much of the world. Be content if even the smallest thing goes a little better, and count that as no small success.
As emperor, Marcus was also Rome's chief priest, and he took part in the old ceremonies. In his notebook he speaks of the gods, but he does not argue about what they are.
In his mind Marcus walks slowly through the crowded court of the first emperor, Augustus. Wife, daughter, friends, doctors and priests, all of them are gone, he notes.
Thinking about death does not seem to make Marcus bitter or afraid. It makes him gentle, patient and more attentive to the day in front of him.
Look at the stars as if you were running with them, wrote Marcus, and think often about the changes of the elements. Seeing life from above, he found, makes the worries of one day look much smaller.
How small a corner of the earth we live in, Marcus tells himself, and how few people will remember us there. The whole earth is only a point in space.
Everything is familiar, Marcus says, and the same things happen again and again. Whoever has seen the present has seen all that ever was or will be.
The same things happen again and again, Marcus says, like the same plays with new actors. Courts, farms, wars and feasts are repeated through the ages.
Wipe away your imaginings, Marcus tells himself, and check your impulses. Quiet your wants, and keep the ruling mind in your own hands.
Marcus divides a person into body, breath of life and mind. The body and the breath only need our care, he says, but the mind is truly our own.
A spider is proud when it catches a fly, Marcus says, and a man is proud when he catches a hare. Another is proud of a small fish, a boar or a bear.
To a wise eye, Marcus says, the shows of the arena and the court look like puppets on strings. They also look like ants carrying crumbs, or like frightened mice scurrying about.
Each person is worth as much as the things he cares about, Marcus says. So choose carefully what you give your attention to.
Think of the public baths, Marcus says: oil, sweat, dirt and greasy water. In the same way, he says, the things of life look unpleasant when we see them plainly.
Waste no more time arguing about what a good person should be, wrote Marcus, but go and be one yourself. Philosophy, for him, was a way of acting and not only a way of talking.
Live as if you were on a mountain, Marcus says. It makes no difference where you live, as long as you live as a citizen of the world.
A doctor always keeps his instruments ready for sudden emergencies, Marcus notes. In the same way, you should keep your principles ready to understand things both divine and human.
A person's true joy, Marcus says, is to do what is human. That means to be kind to others, to ignore bodily urges, to test first impressions and to study nature.
Marcus often tests a planned action by asking himself a few simple questions. Is it needed, and does it serve the people around me?
Wealth and poverty, honour and shame, health and sickness come to good people and bad people alike, Marcus notes. So they cannot be what makes a life good.
O my soul, will you ever be good, simple and whole, Marcus asks. Will you ever be satisfied and want nothing more?
Marcus recalls a poet's line that the wind scatters some leaves on the ground. People, he says, are like leaves, and so are those who praise us.
Do not be troubled by the future, Marcus tells himself. If you must meet it, you will meet it with the same reason you use today.
Enter into the mind of whoever is speaking, Marcus tells himself, and let him enter into yours. Listen with your whole attention to what he really means.

When you are angry, wrote Marcus, remember that the anger and distress hurt you more than the thing that caused them. Soon, he adds, both you and the other person will be dead, and the quarrel will be forgotten.
Kindness is unbeatable, wrote Marcus, if it is real and not just a smile put on for show. What can even the most violent person do to you, he asked, if you stay kind to him?
When angry with someone, Marcus tells himself, remember that you also do many things wrong. You cannot even be sure that the person has done wrong at all.
Gentleness and kindness are more human, and more manly, than rage, Marcus says. Strength and courage belong to the kind person, not the angry one.
When you correct a wrongdoer, Marcus says, do it kindly, in the way a friend would. Do not do it to score a point or to show off.
The thinking soul, Marcus says, sees itself, shapes itself and enjoys its own harvest. Plants and animals, by contrast, have their fruit taken by others.
Tragedies were first put on stage, Marcus notes, to remind us what happens in life. What moves us in a theatre, he says, should not shake us on the larger stage of life.
If anyone can show me that I am wrong, Marcus says, I will gladly change. I am after the truth, and truth has never harmed anyone.
When someone wrongs you, Marcus says, ask what that person thought was good or bad. Once you see this, you will feel pity instead of anger.
Marcus never claims to have mastered his anger, and he does not hide that it troubles him. The length of his lists of reminders shows how often he needed them.
Epictetus taught that each person is an actor given a part by the playwright. It is not our job to choose the part, but to play it well.
Marcus's own part was that of emperor, the biggest in the empire. His notebook reminds him that a role is a costume, and that he must stay himself underneath.

Everything you hope to reach by a long road, wrote Marcus, you can have now if you do not refuse it to yourself. Let the past go, trust the future, and direct the present toward what is just and good.
Marcus wondered why each of us loves himself most, and yet values other people's opinion of him above his own. It is a puzzle that most of us still recognise today.
If it is not right, do not do it, Marcus says, and if it is not true, do not say it. It is one of the simplest rules in the whole book.
Stop wandering about, Marcus tells himself, because you may never read these notes again. Help yourself while there is still time, if you care about yourself.
Return to your senses, Marcus tells himself, and call yourself back. When you wake, see that your troubles were only dreams, and look at the world with the same calm.
Epictetus said that every event has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. If your brother wrongs you, do not take it by the wrong one.
Roman writers say that Marcus listened patiently to legal cases and tried hard to be fair. He is said to have given them long and careful attention.
The calm that Marcus seeks is not the calm of a man with no troubles. It is the calm of a man who has learned how to carry them.
You could leave life right now, Marcus reminds himself, and let that decide what you do, say and think. This is not meant to frighten but to clarify.
You have been a citizen of this great city, Marcus tells himself, and it does not matter whether for three years or five. The law is the same for all, so there is nothing dreadful in leaving.

Marcus compared life to a play in which the director may send you off after three acts instead of five. Those three acts, he wrote, are still the whole drama, and nature has simply decided that it is time to go.
It is no hardship to be sent away from the city, Marcus says, not by a tyrant or an unjust judge, but by Nature. Nature is the same power that brought you in.
The notebook's closing words tell you to go with a good heart. The one who lets you go, Marcus says, is also kind and glad.
Epictetus said never to say that you have lost something, only that you have given it back. Marcus saw life itself as something borrowed that must be returned with thanks.
Nothing that is according to nature is evil, Marcus writes. Dying is as natural as growing up and growing old.
Epictetus said that death is nothing terrible, or it would have seemed terrible to Socrates. The terror, he said, is in the opinion we hold of it.
The notebook ends with that farewell, and with no word of explanation. We do not know whether Marcus planned to write more.
He lives with the gods, Marcus says, who shows them that his soul is content with what it is given. Such a person does what his own best mind asks.
From 169 Marcus lived mostly at the front, while Roman armies fought tribes along the Danube. The enemies included the Marcomanni, the Quadi and the Sarmatians.
A famous story says that a storm saved thirsty Roman soldiers around 172. The sources disagree about who sent the rain, and the details are disputed.
In 175 a general named Avidius Cassius declared himself emperor in the east. His own soldiers killed him within a few months.
Roman writers say that Marcus showed mercy to the rebel's family. They also say he refused to punish those who had written to the rebel.
In 175 his wife Faustina, who had travelled with him, died in a small town in Cappadocia. Marcus mourned her and honoured her memory, and the town was later renamed in her honour.
Ancient writers say that Marcus sold imperial treasures in Trajan's Forum to pay for the war. They say he did this instead of raising taxes.
In 177 Marcus made his teenage son Commodus joint emperor. It is the decision for which he is most often criticised.
The doctor Galen served the imperial household and wrote that Marcus often had stomach and chest pain. He says Marcus took a famous medicine against it.
Marcus died in 180, still on campaign near the Danube, and ancient writers disagree about the exact place. His son Commodus, who had already been named his partner in power, became emperor.
Rome later raised a column with scenes of the northern wars. A bronze statue of Marcus on a horse also survives.
After Marcus died, his private notebook was somehow kept safe. No one knows who saved it, or how it lived long enough to be copied.
Greek scribes copied it by hand over many centuries. A churchman named Arethas owned a copy around the year 900 and wrote about it.
In 1559 the first printed edition came out in Zurich, edited by the scholar Wilhelm Xylander. After that, the book began to spread across Europe.
Meric Casaubon made the first English translation, which was published in 1634. Since then the book has been translated into many languages.
The Meditations is not a story, and it is not a textbook either. It is a notebook of short thoughts, and Marcus often repeats himself because he is reminding himself of the same lessons.
Marcus was an emperor who fought long wars, and he was not a perfect man. His notes read less like a saint's boast than like the work of a person who keeps trying to improve.
Kings, soldiers, poets and ordinary people have all turned to the notebook. The king Frederick the Great of Prussia is said to have admired it greatly.
Readers in many countries still turn to the Meditations, because its advice is short and honest. Its subjects, such as anger, fear, tiredness and loss, are as familiar today as they were in Rome.
Many readers keep a notebook of their own, as Marcus did, and write down what they want to remember. A few honest lines each morning or evening may help to bring back calm.
The Meditations never says that life is easy, but it offers a few steady ideas about thoughts, duty, kindness and acceptance. Each morning, Marcus seems to say, we can begin again.
C1C2: Marcus Aurelius governed the Roman Empire from the year 161 until his death in 180, at a time of frontier wars and a deadly plague, and yet he is remembered less as a ruler than as a thinker. A follower of Stoicism, the ancient Greek school of philosophy that taught calm, self-control and duty, he kept a private notebook in which he wrote reminders to himself. Those notes, now known as the Meditations, have been read for centuries by people who have never cared about Rome at all.

The notes are written in Greek, which was then the language of philosophy, and they are divided into twelve books of unequal length. At the end of two of the books, a line says where they were written, in the camps along the Danube frontier where Marcus spent much of his later reign. They were almost certainly never meant to be published, and the title Meditations was added long afterwards, since the Greek title found in the manuscripts means simply To Himself.

Nothing in the notebook suggests that Marcus expected a single stranger to read it, and its tone is that of a man talking quietly with himself. The Greek title found in the manuscripts means simply To Himself, and the familiar name Meditations was attached long afterwards by editors and publishers. That privacy is the book's great charm, for a man who writes only for himself has no reason to pose, to boast or to hide his doubts.

Marcus was born in Rome in 121, into a rich and respected family that had come originally from Spain. His father died while the boy was still very young, and he was brought up in the household of his grandfather, a man he later remembered with gratitude. Looking back, Marcus would credit this old relative with teaching him good character and a steady temper.

The emperor Hadrian, who ruled Rome at the time, noticed the earnest boy and, according to ancient writers, favoured him from an early age. He is said to have nicknamed him Verissimus, a play on the family name Verus that means the most truthful. Whether or not the story is exactly true, it fits the picture of a child who took honesty and learning very seriously.

As Hadrian grew old and ill, he searched for a worthy heir, and in 138 he chose a calm and respected senator named Antoninus Pius. He made one condition, which was that Pius must adopt two young people, and one of them was Marcus, then sixteen years old. At a stroke, the quiet boy from a good family became the likely future ruler of the Roman world.

Antoninus Pius ruled for twenty-three years, and they were among the calmest years in Roman history, with few wars and a steady, careful government. Marcus served at his side, sat in his councils, held high office and learned how an emperor really spends his days. In 145 he also married the emperor's daughter, Faustina, and the couple would have a large family.

When Antoninus Pius died in 161, Marcus was the natural heir, and he could easily have ruled alone. Instead he insisted that his adoptive brother Lucius Verus should share the throne, and for the first time Rome had two emperors with the same title. Verus was lively and fond of pleasure, while Marcus was serious and hard-working, yet the two men governed together until Verus died in 169.

Soon the new emperors faced disaster, for around 165 soldiers returning from the war against Parthia in the east carried a deadly plague into the empire. It spread along the roads and sea routes from city to city, and a great many people died, though no one knows exactly how many. Marcus lived with this fear for the rest of his reign, and its shadow can be felt in his many reminders that life is short.

Soon war came to the northern frontier, where tribes such as the Marcomanni and the Quadi crossed the Danube and threatened the Roman provinces. Marcus, who had never been a soldier by temperament, left Rome and spent much of the rest of his life in army camps along the river. It was in those cold, crowded places that some of the notebook was written, and the calm of its pages is all the more remarkable for that.

Stoicism began in Athens around 300 BC, when a merchant from Cyprus named Zeno started to teach philosophy to anyone who would listen. He spoke under a painted porch, called a stoa in Greek, and his followers were soon known as the people of the porch. The school lasted for about five centuries, and by the time of Marcus it had become the favourite philosophy of many serious Romans.

At the heart of Stoicism is a simple division of the world into what is up to us and what is not. Our judgments, intentions and actions belong to the first group, while health, reputation, the weather and the behaviour of other people belong to the second, and the Stoic's task is to care most about the first. Marcus returns to this idea so often in his notebook that it can be seen as the thread that holds the whole book together.

The Stoics taught that there are four great virtues, which are wisdom, justice, courage and self-control, and that a person's goodness is measured by these alone. Wisdom sees what is true, justice gives each person his due, courage faces danger and pain, and self-control resists the pull of pleasure. Marcus returns to these four again and again in his notebook, as a sailor returns to the stars.

For the Stoics, nature was not only trees and rivers but the rational order that runs through the whole universe, and human beings are the part of it that can think. To live well, therefore, is to use reason, to accept the world as it is and to play one's own part in it faithfully. Marcus often tells himself to do exactly that, whether the subject is a hard morning or a hard death.

Epictetus was born a slave, lame in one leg, and after he gained his freedom he became one of the most respected teachers of Stoic philosophy. He taught in Greece, and a student named Arrian wrote down his lessons so carefully that we can almost hear him speaking. So far as we know, Marcus never met him, for Epictetus lived a generation earlier, but he quotes him several times and plainly treated him as a master.

The Stoics believed that the whole universe is like one great city, shared by gods and human beings alike, and that every person is a citizen of it, whatever country he was born in. This was a bold idea in an age of walls and frontiers, and Marcus took it to heart. It gave him a reason to think of the good of the whole human family and not only of the interests of Rome.

According to the Stoics, things like wealth, fame, health and pleasure are not good or bad in themselves, because good and bad people can have them in equal measure. What truly makes a life good is character, and character is built from our own choices and judgments. This was a hard teaching for an emperor who had more wealth and power than almost anyone in the world, and he writes about it with the humility of a man who knows how much he has to lose.

For the Stoics, philosophy was not a subject to be studied and forgotten but a way of life to be practised every day, much as an athlete trains his body. Some Stoics reviewed their day each evening, and others imagined future troubles in advance so as not to be surprised by them. Marcus's notebook belongs to the same tradition, for it is a set of short, practical reminders, written to keep his own mind steady in the middle of heavy duties.

In the notebook Marcus often speaks to himself as you, and the voice that results is surprisingly human, for he scolds, encourages and sometimes gives himself orders like a coach. He rarely claims to have reached wisdom, and he is often hard on himself for small failings of patience or attention. It is this honesty, more than any single idea, that has made readers feel that they know the man.

The twelve books of the notebook are not an argument that builds from one chapter to the next, but a collection of notes added over many years, some long and some only a line or two. Ideas come back again and again, sometimes in almost the same words, because Marcus kept returning to the lessons that he found hardest to learn. This retelling will take the books one at a time, in their order, and will stop now and then to meet the man behind them.

The first book is different from all the others, for it is not advice to himself but a long list of thanks. One by one Marcus names the people who shaped him, from his family and teachers to the emperor who adopted him, and says what he learned from each. It is a lesson in gratitude, and it also gives us a portrait of the Roman world in which a future emperor was brought up.

The first person Marcus thanks is his grandfather Verus, from whom he says he learned good character and the government of his temper. A calm temper is not a gift that everyone is born with, and Marcus seems to have gained it by watching a man he loved and trusted. The thanks are short, but they show how seriously he took the question of how character is passed on from one generation to the next.

Marcus hardly knew his father, who died when the boy was very young, and so he knew him mainly through the memory that others kept and the good name that he left behind. From these, he says, he took modesty and a manly character, which Romans valued very highly. It is a touching thought that a man can be a teacher to his son simply by being remembered well.

From his mother Lucilla, Marcus says, he learned reverence for the gods and the habit of giving freely to others. She also taught him to avoid not only wrongdoing but even the thought of it, and to live simply, far from the luxuries that wealth offered. For the son of a rich family, this was an unusual and valuable education.

Marcus then thanks his great-grandfather, who taught him that a child should have good teachers at home rather than attend the public schools. He also taught him that for such an education one must spend generously, however much it costs. It is a lesson that fits well with the long list of tutors and teachers who come next.

A tutor named Diognetus taught the young Marcus not to waste his time on trifles, and not to be taken in by the miracle-workers and magicians who then did good business. He also encouraged the boy to write dialogues and to take up the Greek way of life, which meant a hard bed with a rough animal skin to sleep under. It is odd to picture a future emperor choosing such discomfort, but it was meant to teach him that he could do without luxury.

Among the teachers whom he remembers, Marcus names Rusticus, who taught him that his character needed training and who warned him against showing off. Rusticus also lent him his own copy of the discourses of Epictetus, a former slave who had become one of the most respected Stoic teachers of his age. It is a touching detail, since it shows an emperor remembering, years later, the kindness of lending a book.

Rusticus gave Marcus more than a book, for he taught him that his character needed training and care, and that a philosopher should never show off. He taught the young man to write his letters in a plain style, to forgive those who had offended him as soon as they wished to make peace, and to read carefully instead of being satisfied with a quick glance. Many a modern student, buried in notes and summaries, could still make good use of that last piece of advice.

Apollonius, a Stoic teacher from the Greek East, showed Marcus what freedom of mind looks like in a real person. He was steady and gentle at once, he looked to reason alone in everything he did, and he stayed the same in sharp pain, in the loss of a child and in long illness. Marcus also admired his patience as a teacher, for he never seemed to resent a pupil's slowness.

From Sextus, Marcus says, he learned kindness and the example of a household that was ruled with a father's love rather than with fear. Sextus was natural without being false, he looked after his friends, and he was patient with people who spoke without thinking or knew very little. He was so pleasant to talk to that the young Marcus remembered his conversation as better than any flattery.

Alexander, a grammarian, taught Marcus a lesson in good manners that every teacher should know. When someone used a wrong word, he never scolded or sneered, but simply used the right word in his own reply, as if he were discussing the subject and not the mistake. The person was corrected without being shamed, and Marcus took the idea far beyond the matter of grammar.

Marcus Cornelius Fronto was the most admired teacher of speech in Rome, and he became a close friend and a lifelong correspondent of his pupil. From him Marcus says he learned to see how much envy, double dealing and pretence there is in a tyrant, and how cold the noble families of Rome can be toward their own relatives. These were useful lessons for a young man who would one day hold more power than anyone in the empire.

Alexander the Platonist taught Marcus never to say, too often or without real need, that he had no time, and never to use the pressure of work as an excuse for neglecting the people around him. It was a hard rule for a man whose desk was never empty, and Marcus kept it with more success than most rulers. Roman writers later noted that he was patient with petitions and legal cases, even when they reached him in the middle of a war.

Catulus, another of his teachers, taught Marcus not to brush aside a friend's complaint, even when the friend seemed to be wrong. The right answer, he said, was to listen and to try to bring the friend back to his usual good humour. He also taught Marcus to speak warmly of his teachers and to show real affection for his own children, which is a pleasing detail in a book about duty.

Severus gave Marcus a love of family, truth and justice, and introduced him to the memory of brave men of the past who had stood up to tyrants. From him Marcus took the idea of a state in which all people are equal before the law and free to speak, and of a ruler who respects that freedom above all. It is a striking thought for an emperor to record, and it shows what kind of ruler he hoped to be.

Maximus was one of the people Marcus admired most, for he seemed to govern himself without effort. He stayed cheerful in every circumstance and even in illness, he was both gentle and dignified, and he did the work in front of him without complaint. Everyone believed that he meant what he said, and Marcus clearly saw in him the kind of man he wanted to become.

Marcus devoted one of the longest portraits in the first book to Antoninus Pius, the emperor who had adopted him and ruled before him. He remembered a man who was firm once a decision was made but never hasty in making it, who listened to advice, disliked flattery, and lived modestly in spite of his power. Much of what Marcus asks of himself in the rest of the book can be traced to this example, and the portrait suggests that he tried to rule as his adoptive father had done.

From Antoninus Pius, Marcus learned to make decisions after careful thought and then to hold to them without wavering. He learned to be gentle with people but firm in purpose, to take no pride in honours that were offered, and to love work and steady effort. He also saw how Pius listened to anyone who had useful advice for the common good, and gave each person what he deserved.

Pius lived plainly for a man who ruled the world, and Marcus remembered details that show it. He often dined at home with his friends, he never demanded that they follow him on every journey, and when they stayed behind they found him exactly the same on his return. He used the pleasures that fortune gave him without pride, and he did not miss them on the days when they were absent.

The first book closes with a long thanksgiving to the gods for his good grandfathers, parents, teachers, friends and family. He thanks them especially for a brother whose character challenged him to improve and whose affection was a pleasure, for a wife who was loving and unpretentious, and for children who were healthy and sound. A last line says that the book was written among the Quadi, on the river Gran, a reminder that all this gratitude was set down in a camp on the edge of a war.

The second book opens with advice to start each day by expecting trouble, since you will meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, jealous and unfriendly.
