Marcus does not say this to make himself bitter, however, but to prepare himself for the day without surprise and without anger. Such people act as they do, he reasons, because they cannot tell good from evil, and so they cannot truly harm a person who can.

Having listed the difficult people he will meet, Marcus adds a reassurance that is the heart of the whole book. None of them, he says, can harm him, because no one can force him to do anything shameful, and so his character remains his own. Their behaviour may be annoying or unfair, but it can only change him if he allows it to.

People, Marcus believed, are made for cooperation, just as the feet, the hands, the eyelids and the two rows of teeth are made to work together. To quarrel with another person or to turn away from him is therefore to act against our own nature. It is a strong argument for kindness, because it treats kindness not as a luxury but as the way human beings are meant to live.

Whatever I am, Marcus tells himself, it is a little flesh, a little breath and the part of me that rules. It is a modest way for an emperor to describe himself, and the next line is even more direct, for he orders himself to throw away his books and not to be distracted any longer. The man who wrote it was surrounded by scrolls and advisers, and he seems to have known how easily reading can replace living.

Remember how long you have been postponing this, Marcus tells himself, and how often the gods have offered you an opportunity that you failed to use. Now is the time to grasp what kind of universe you belong to, and what intelligence governs it, before your own span runs out. If you neglect it, the moment will pass, and you will pass with it, and the opportunity will never return.

Marcus often reminds himself that life is short and that its end may come at any moment, and he treats this not as a gloomy thought but as a spur to action. You could leave life right now, he writes, so let that decide what you do and say and think. He also tells himself to do each task as though it were his last, with a serious and simple dignity, and not to waste a single hour in drifting.

In one of his sternest passages Marcus turns on his own soul, saying that it is insulting itself and will soon have no chance left to honour itself. Life is short for everyone, he writes, and his is nearly finished, yet he is looking for his happiness in the opinions of other people. The words are all the more striking when we remember that the man speaking was cheered by crowds and flattered by courtiers.

Marcus uses a plain image of a branch that has been cut from the branch beside it, and is therefore cut off from the whole tree. A person who turns against others, or who pulls away in anger or contempt, has done the same to himself, and has separated himself from the community of mankind. He adds that, unlike a real branch, a human being can grow back, for it is always in his power to return and become part of the whole again.

In a passage of striking bleakness, Marcus describes a human life as a mere point in time, set in the middle of a world that is never still. The body is a stream, the mind a dream and a vapour, and life itself a battle and a short stay in a foreign land, while the fame that follows is soon forgotten. Yet his conclusion is not despair but a call to live by one's principles, since the only thing that can guide a person through such a world, he says, is philosophy.

Book two ends with a short note giving the name of the place where it was written, which is Carnuntum, a large Roman camp and town on the Danube east of the modern city of Vienna. Marcus is known to have spent part of the northern wars there, and the note shows him writing in the middle of a military base. It is a reminder that these gentle reflections on patience and death were composed within sight of an army.

Book three opens with a sobering thought, which is that life is being used up every day and a smaller part of it is left. Marcus adds that if a man lives to a great age, it is not certain that his mind will stay sharp enough to understand the world and to do his duty. For that reason, he says, we should not put off our best efforts until some calmer year that may never come.

Marcus warns himself not to spend the rest of his life in thoughts about other people, unless the thoughts serve some common good. Wondering what a neighbour is doing, what he is saying, what he is plotting and why, drags the mind away from its own proper work. He wanted a mind that was steady and watchful over itself, one that could say plainly where its own duty lay.

In a passage that is both grim and calming, Marcus makes a list of the great men who have died. Hippocrates, the famous doctor, cured many diseases and then fell ill and died himself, and the conquerors Alexander and Pompey, who had destroyed whole cities and defeated great armies, also departed from life. The point is plain, for if death reached the greatest healers and the greatest warriors, no one should be astonished when it comes for him.

In one of his gentlest passages, Marcus observes that even the accidental by-products of nature have a charm of their own. The cracks on the crust of a loaf of bread, the figs that split open at the height of their ripeness, and the ears of corn that bend toward the ground are all, he says, strangely pleasing to the eye. A person with a real feeling for nature, he adds, will find beauty almost everywhere.

To the example of the cracked loaf Marcus adds others, such as figs that gape open when they are very ripe and olives that are close to falling from the tree. Even the ears of corn that bend under their own weight and the frowning brow of a lion, he says, have a beauty of their own. Anyone with a feeling for nature, he adds, will find such things pleasing, and that includes the lines of age in a human face.

In a passage full of Roman pride, Marcus tells himself to do every act as a Roman and a man should, with seriousness, kindness and a sense of duty. He pictures himself as a soldier at his post, ready to leave life the moment the signal sounds. Such a man needs no oath and no witness, for he is waiting only for the call, and he has nothing to hide.

Never value as a benefit, Marcus advises, anything that will force you to break your word, to lose your self-respect, to hate or suspect another person or to act a part. Anyone who prefers his own mind and its goodness to such gains, he says, needs no stage, no walls and no curtains to hide behind. He can live among others or alone, and he will not even care how long he lives.

Marcus gives himself a method that anyone can use, which is to ask of every impression what it is in itself, to strip away its decoration and to name its parts. Seen this way, he says, the things that dazzle us may turn out to be much smaller than they first appeared. The same method can calm our fears, for terrors, too, shrink when we look at them plainly.

Marcus tells himself to do whatever is in front of him with care, seriousness, energy and a calm heart, free of every other distraction. He would keep the spirit within him pure, he says, as if he might be required to give it back at any moment. That, he thinks, is the secret of doing small things well, and it makes a quiet task as worthy as a grand one.

If you do these things, Marcus concludes, and are content with the present, speaking the truth and acting with honour in every word and deed, you will live well, and no one can prevent it. Fate may take a person's health, wealth or reputation, but it cannot take the quiet success of having acted rightly. It is a promise that comes from a man who knew very well how much fate could do.

In the fourth book Marcus notes that people are always seeking retreats for themselves, in houses in the country, on sea shores or in the hills, and he admits that he too has often longed for them. Yet this, he says, is a very ordinary kind of wish, because the retreat that is truly available is a different one. The surprise is that a man who could have lived in any palace in the empire should have written such a thing.

People are always longing for a retreat, Marcus writes, in the countryside, by the sea or among the mountains, and he admits that this is a very common wish. Yet at any hour you can withdraw into your own mind, he says, and nowhere has a person a quieter or more untroubled refuge than in his own soul. He advises keeping a few short, clear principles ready there, so that they can send him back to his work cleansed of all complaint.

Marcus names the short principles that he likes to keep ready, and the first is that outside things cannot touch the mind, which is calm in itself and disturbed only by its own opinions. The second is that everything he can see will soon change and cease to be, and that he has already witnessed many such changes in his own lifetime. Taken together, he says, they teach that the universe is change and that life is opinion.

Marcus offers a short chain of thought at the centre of Stoic practice, which is that if you take away the opinion that you have been harmed, the complaint goes with it, and the harm goes too. He does not deny that bad things happen, for loss and pain are plainly real. He claims instead that much of our suffering comes from the judgments that we add to events, and that those judgments are ours to change.

Do few things, says one philosopher whom Marcus quotes, if you want to be tranquil, and Marcus adds that it is better still to do only what is necessary and to do it well. The greater part of what we say and do is not needed, he points out, and a person who removes it will gain both leisure and peace of mind. On every occasion, therefore, he should ask himself whether this is one of the unnecessary things.

Time, Marcus writes, is a kind of river made up of passing events, and its current is so strong that no sooner is a thing brought into sight than it is swept away and another takes its place. That second thing will in turn be carried off, and so on without end. The picture is meant to cure us of our attachment to the things we cling to most, and it teaches us not to treat small troubles as if they would last for ever.

Be like a headland, Marcus tells himself, against which the waves break again and again, while it stands firm and the water around it falls quiet. It is a fine image of steadiness, and it comes with a pointed question about how we describe our own misfortunes. I am unlucky that this has happened to me, he imagines someone saying, but he answers that he is lucky, because he can bear it without being crushed by the present or afraid of the future.

Marcus compares the mind that is in harmony with nature to a blazing fire, which consumes whatever is thrown into it and grows higher and brighter as a result. In the same way, he says, the steady mind turns every obstacle into material for its own use, and what was meant to be a hindrance becomes fuel. It is an optimistic picture, though a demanding one, since it asks that we meet each setback as an opportunity.

In a short and cheerful prayer, Marcus addresses the universe directly and tells it that whatever suits it also suits him. Nothing that comes in its right time, he says, is too early or too late for him. Everything that the seasons of nature bring is fruit to him, since all things come from nature, exist in nature and return to nature, and a person who accepts this has nothing left to complain about.

Do not act as if you were going to live for ten thousand years, Marcus tells himself, for death hangs over you. While you still live, and while it is still in your power, be good, and do it now. The advice is not gloomy, though it may sound so, for it turns the fact of death into a reason to begin at once.

Marcus asks us to think of whole cities that have vanished, and among them he seems to name Pompeii and Herculaneum, which were buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in the year 79. If a town full of shops, houses and busy people can disappear in a single day, he suggests, then no single life can claim to be safe or permanent. The thought is meant to loosen our grip on the things we guard so anxiously.

Marcus asks himself to consider the days of the emperor Vespasian, about a century before his own, and to picture what people did then. They married and raised children, fell ill and died, fought wars, traded, farmed, flattered one another, plotted, grumbled and saved up treasure, and all of that busy life has now vanished without a trace. Our own concerns, he suggests, will fade in exactly the same way, and this should help us to put our worries in proportion.

In a short time you will be nobody and nowhere, Marcus tells himself, and the same is true of Hadrian and Augustus, the men who made and ruled the empire. The point is not meant to make him sad, but to take the shine off the idea of greatness, since even the most powerful names fade into history. If they have faded, a lesser person has little reason to worry about being remembered.

A man who is passionate about his fame after death, Marcus writes, forgets that everyone who remembers him will also die very soon, and so will those who come after them, until the memory is extinguished completely. It is a surprising thought coming from an emperor, whose name and image were on coins and statues throughout the empire. Yet he uses it not to feel sad but to teach himself to do right for its own sake and not for the praise.

A man who longs for fame after his death, Marcus writes, forgets that everyone who remembers him will soon die as well, and so will the next generation, and the next. In the end the memory is extinguished, passed along through a chain of people who admire for a while and then perish. The thought is sobering, but it also frees us from the fear of being forgotten, which is a fear that nobody has ever escaped.

Marcus asks himself to think of the whole of matter and the whole of time, and to see what small part of each has been given to him. He is a tiny portion of a great mass, and his life is a short moment in an enormous stretch of years. This does not make him despair, but it does teach him that most of his worries are far too big for the space they take up.

The universe loves to change things and to make new ones like them, Marcus writes, and everything that exists is in some way the seed of what will come next. It is like a seed that falls into the earth and comes up again as a plant. He draws comfort from this, for it means that nothing is truly destroyed, and the end of one thing is always the beginning of another.

Pass through this little span of time in agreement with nature, Marcus advises, and end it cheerfully, as an olive falls when it is ripe, thanking the tree that grew it. It is one of the most graceful images in the book, and it shows how a man may meet death without bitterness. The same picture holds for the end of a day, a task or a season of life.

Whatever is beautiful, Marcus argues, is beautiful in itself, and praise is no part of it, for a thing is made neither better nor worse by being admired. Gold, ivory, a flower, a jewel or a well-made tool does not improve when the crowd applauds it, and it does not spoil when the crowd looks away. If that is true of things, it is truer still of people, whose worth does not depend on what is said about them.

From all these reminders about dust and forgetting, Marcus draws a lesson that is simple to state and hard to follow. Stop craving fame, which is only the noise of people who will soon be gone, and do the work that is in front of you with honour. A good life, in his view, is not measured by what others will say of it, but by whether its owner acted well while he had the chance.

At dawn, when he found it hard to get out of bed, Marcus reminded himself that he was getting up to do the work of a human being. Why should he complain, he asked, about starting the very task that he was born for and brought into the world to do? Was he made to lie under the blankets and keep himself warm, he wondered, and the question has made many a reluctant reader smile.

Marcus points to the small creatures around him, the plants and little birds, the ants, spiders and bees, which all do their own work and so help to put the world in order. Each of them is doing what it was made for, and none of them stays in bed. He asks himself, with a kind of gentle shame, how a human being could refuse to do his.

The lazy voice in his head has an answer ready, which is that it is more pleasant to stay where he is. Marcus does not deny the pleasure, but he asks whether he exists only to enjoy himself, and not for action and effort. The little dialogue is one of the most human moments in the book, and it is easy to imagine him having it on a cold morning in a camp on the Danube.

Marcus describes three kinds of people who do a good turn for another person, and the differences between them are instructive. The first is ready to count it as a favour that must be repaid, while the second does not say so but privately thinks of the other as a debtor. The third is like a vine that has borne its grapes and asks for nothing more, and this is the kind that Marcus wants to be.

How easy it is, Marcus writes, to push away every troublesome or unsuitable impression and at once to be perfectly calm. He treats the mind as a slate that can be wiped clean, and he suggests that it is only habit and fear that make us think otherwise. This is a bold claim, and he does not pretend that it is always easy, for the reminder appears in the notebook again and again.

Marcus compares the mind to a piece of cloth, for the soul, he says, is dyed by its thoughts. Whatever thoughts you have most often, he warns, will shape the character of your mind. He therefore urges himself to keep dipping it in worthy ones, and the image is a useful reminder that the stories we repeat inwardly slowly become who we are.

What stands in the way, Marcus writes, becomes the way, since the obstacle to an action can be turned into a means of advancing it. A difficulty that blocks one virtue calls for another, so that a delay becomes a lesson in patience and an insult becomes a chance to show calm. This is perhaps the most quoted of his sayings today, and it sums up the Stoic habit of making use of whatever life puts before us.

When we say that a doctor has ordered a certain person to take a walk, a cold bath or some rest, Marcus points out, we accept it without complaint, because we trust that it is for his health. In the same spirit, he says, we should accept whatever nature prescribes, whether it is illness, loss or hardship, since it is also meant for the good of the whole. The medicine of life is often bitter, but a wise patient drinks it with some gratitude.

Do not be disgusted with yourself, or discouraged, or dissatisfied, Marcus writes, if you do not manage to act well in everything. When you fail, he says, simply return to your task, and be content if most of what you do is truly worthy of a human being. It is a surprisingly gentle rule from a man with so many duties, and it shows that Stoic discipline was not meant to be cruel.

Marcus, who is rarely playful, even allows himself a joke, though it is a very dry one. If a person's breath or armpits smell bad, he asks, what is the use of being angry, since such a mouth and such armpits must produce such a smell? The humour has a serious purpose, for it reminds us that people are what they are, and that to be furious about their nature is as foolish as to scold the weather.

Marcus gives himself a short list of things that should not matter so long as he is doing his duty: whether he is cold or warm, drowsy or well rested, praised or criticised, dying or busy with something else. Duty, in other words, does not wait for comfortable conditions, and a task is no less important because it is performed at a bad hour. For a man who spent years in army camps on a cold frontier, it was a lesson that came from daily life.

Marcus adds a startling thought to his rule about duty, which is that dying, too, is one of the acts of life. If a person has spent his days doing what was right, the last act deserves the same calm attention as all the others. It is a very practical way of looking at death, as one more task to be done properly, with neither fuss nor fear.

The best way of taking revenge, Marcus writes, is not to become like the person who has wronged you. When we answer cruelty with cruelty, or lies with lies, we simply add a second wrong to the first and become part of the problem that we complain about. His advice is therefore both moral and practical, because it frees us from carrying another person's bad behaviour around inside ourselves.

Alexander the Great and his mule driver, Marcus observes, were brought to the same condition by death, for either they were taken back into the life-giving order of the universe or both were scattered into atoms. A conqueror who had ruled much of the known world and a man who cared for his animals ended up in the same place. The comparison humbles the proud and consoles the humble, and Marcus applies it first of all to himself.

When you are faced with delicious food, Marcus advises, tell yourself plainly that this is the body of a dead fish or a dead bird, and that the famous wine is only a little grape juice. The purple robe of an emperor, he adds, is merely sheep's wool dyed with the liquid of a shellfish. The exercise strips away the glamour that our minds attach to things, and it helps us to see them without craving them, which is exactly what a ruler surrounded by luxury needed to practise.

My nature is reasonable and made for community, Marcus writes, and my city and country, as Antoninus, the name he bore as emperor, is Rome, while as a human being it is the world. Whatever helps these two cities is the only thing that is truly good for me, and whatever harms them cannot be a good at all. This was a useful rule for an emperor, since it forced him to weigh every decision against the whole human family as well as the Roman state.

See that you do not become a Caesar, Marcus warns himself, and do not be dyed with that dye, for such things happen to people who hold great power. Keep yourself simple, good, pure, serious, free from pretence, a friend of justice and kind to others. Few men in his position have written so plainly about the way power can change a person.

What is not good for the swarm, Marcus writes, is not good for the bee. For him this short saying was a whole philosophy of community, since he believed that every human being is a part of a larger body and cannot truly flourish at its expense. A ruler responsible for millions of people had every reason to think in this way, and it gives his private notes a public purpose.

Do not suppose that something is impossible, Marcus tells himself, merely because you find it hard. If a thing is possible and proper for a human being, believe that it lies within your own reach as well. It is a short and bracing rule, and anyone who has put off a difficult task will recognise the temptation that it is meant to answer.

Marcus does not pretend to know how the universe is run, and in one passage he sets out the possibilities side by side. If there is an unavoidable fate, he says, there is no point resisting it, and if there is a kind providence, he should make himself worthy of its help. If there is only a confusion without a ruler, he can still be glad that he carries within himself an intelligence that rules.

Love only what happens to you, Marcus writes, for it is spun with the thread of your own destiny, and what could be more suitable? The Stoics believed that the universe is ordered by reason, and so they taught that a wise person should accept events with a good will and not with resentment. It is a demanding idea, and some readers find it comforting while others find it hard to accept, but it is central to the way Marcus lived.

Marcus tells himself to take delight and rest in a single thing, which is to pass from one helpful act to the next, always keeping the gods in mind. It is a plain recipe for contentment, and it takes away the burden of waiting for some distant reward. Pleasure, in this account, is not a prize at the end of work but the quiet satisfaction that goes along with it.

Marcus imagines an emerald speaking, and it says that whatever anyone does or says, it must be an emerald and keep its colour. He applies the thought to himself, so that whatever people do or say, he must remain good and be himself. The jewel does not change its colour to please the crowd, and a person of character should be just as steady.

Look within, Marcus tells himself, for within is the fountain of all that is good, and it will never cease to bubble up so long as you keep digging. The image is one of patient work, since a spring may be hidden beneath dry ground and reached only through effort. It encourages the reader to believe that the resources needed for a good life are not far away and are not for sale.

Pain, Marcus writes, is neither unbearable nor unending, provided that you remember its limits and do not enlarge it with your imagination. He is not denying that suffering is real, and ancient writers say that he suffered from poor health himself, but he is pointing to the extra layer of fear and complaint that the mind can pile on top of it. The idea is a Stoic attitude of mind and not a medical claim, and anyone in real pain should of course seek proper care.

In the art of living, Marcus says, a person should be more like a wrestler than a gladiator, because the gladiator depends on a weapon that may be taken away. A man who loses his sword is in great danger, but a wrestler always has his hands and needs only to use them. Our skills of mind and character, he suggests, are like the wrestler's hands, since nobody can take them from us unless we give them up.

It is a special feature of human beings, Marcus says, to love even those who do wrong. This becomes possible when we remember that such people are our relatives, that they act from ignorance and not from choice, and that soon both of us will be dead. Above all, he adds, the wrongdoer has not really harmed us, since he has not made our mind any worse.

Do not be ashamed to be helped, Marcus tells himself, for your task is to do your duty like a soldier in the assault on a town wall. If you are lame and cannot climb to the top alone, but can do it with the help of a comrade, then you should take the help gladly. For a proud man in a high office this is a humble lesson, and it is one that many leaders never learn.

This is the perfection of character, Marcus says, to live out each day as if it were the last, without violent excitement, without dullness of spirit and without any kind of pretence. It does not mean that we should live recklessly, as if nothing mattered, but that we should live fully, as if everything did. A person who really tries this will find that the ordinary day becomes more precious, and so does the ordinary person.

All things, Marcus writes, are woven together, and the bond between them is holy, so that hardly anything is wholly unconnected with anything else. In his view the universe is a single living order, and every person has a small part to play in it. To see oneself in this way is to feel less alone and more responsible, and it is one reason that his notes keep returning to duty and kindness.

The mind that is free from passion, Marcus writes, is a citadel, for a person has nothing more secure to which he can flee for refuge. Whoever has not seen this is ignorant, he says, and whoever has seen it and does not take shelter there is unhappy. A citadel was the strongest part of an ancient city, and for a man who spent his life in camps and councils the image of an inner fortress must have had a special appeal.

In a moment of honesty Marcus admits that he has fallen short of the philosopher's life, and that his position as emperor makes it hard for others to see him as a philosopher at all. The life of court and camp stands in his way, and he accepts that he must let this wish go. What matters, he decides, is to live out the rest of his days as nature wants, and not to worry about the opinions of others.

Marcus sets the great conquerors Alexander, Caesar and Pompey beside the thinkers Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates, and he prefers the thinkers. The philosophers, he says, saw the nature of things and understood their causes, while the generals had so many cares and were slaves to so many things. It is a striking judgment for an emperor to make, since he was himself the heir of the power that Caesar had won.

If a cucumber is bitter, Marcus advises, you simply throw it away, and if there are brambles in the road, you turn aside from them. That is enough, he says, and you should not go on to ask why such things were ever made. The little scene shows his practical side, since it teaches us to deal calmly with the annoyances of life instead of arguing with the universe about them.

Human beings exist for the sake of one another, Marcus writes, and so we must either teach them or bear with them. The advice gives us two choices only, and neither of them is anger, contempt or a cold withdrawal. It is a good rule for anyone who must live and work among people who disappoint them, and it is easy to imagine an emperor repeating it to himself after a long day of petitions.

If you are pained by anything outside you, Marcus writes, it is not the thing itself that disturbs you but your own judgment about it, and it is in your power to wipe out that judgment at once. He does not say that bad things do not happen, but that the harm lives in what we tell ourselves about them. It is the same idea as the one in the fourth book, and Marcus repeats it because he knew how quickly we forget it.

Marcus borrows from older philosophers the image of the mind as a perfect sphere, which keeps its shape when it is neither stretched out toward things nor shrunk inward upon itself. Such a mind is not scattered by desire or collapsed by fear, but is lit by the light that shows it the truth. It is a hard picture to live up to, but it describes very well what a calm and clear person feels like.

Do not disturb yourself by picturing your whole life at once, Marcus advises, nor by imagining all the troubles that might come. When a difficulty arises, ask what is truly unbearable in it, and you will usually be ashamed to find that it is small. Neither the past nor the future can hurt you, he adds, but only the present, which shrinks when you mark out its limits.

Marcus plays on two Greek words that sound almost alike, the word for a part and the word for a limb. If you only say that you are a part of humanity, he explains, you do not yet love people from the heart, and you do good only as a duty. If you say that you are a limb, you feel the unity of the body, and you do good for the joy of it and not for reward.

Marcus offers a short argument that sounds like a joke but is meant seriously. Wherever it is possible to live, he reasons, it is possible to live well, and since it is possible to live in a palace, it must be possible to live well in a palace as well. He was reminding himself that wealth and power are not an excuse for a bad life, any more than poverty is.

He who does wrong, Marcus writes, does wrong to himself, because by acting badly he makes himself into a worse person. The thought can be a comfort, since it means that the wrongdoer is already paying a price that no one else can see, and so there is little point in being angry with him. It is a very Stoic idea, and it helps to explain why Marcus tried to answer injustice with patience and not with rage.

Acting unjustly is a kind of impiety, Marcus argues, because nature has made thinking beings for the sake of one another, to help one another according to their worth and never to harm one another. A person who breaks this law therefore sins against the order of the universe itself, and not merely against his neighbour. For an emperor who judged cases every day, the idea gave justice a sacred weight.

Do not despise death, Marcus writes, but be content with it, since it too is one of the things that nature wills. He compares it to the other changes of a lifetime, such as the growth of teeth, the first beard and the first grey hairs, all of which belong to the natural order. His calm attitude is not coldness but an attempt to meet the one certain event of every life without panic.

Marcus compares death with birth, which is a surprising choice, since both, he says, are mysteries of nature and changes of the same elements. As a person waits with patience for the moment when a child will come out of its mother, he writes, so he should be ready for the hour when his own soul will leave the body that wraps it. The thought is not cheerful, but it is steadying, because it makes the end of life seem no stranger than its beginning.

Marcus writes that the one thing that might hold him back from leaving life is the hope of living with people who share his principles. Yet he sees how much trouble there is in the discord of ordinary life with others, so much that he is ready to say that death can come quickly. It is a rare moment of weariness in the notebook, and it makes his steadiness elsewhere seem even more remarkable.

When you are offended by someone's shamelessness, Marcus tells himself, ask whether it is possible that shameless people should not exist in the world. It is not possible, he concludes, so you should not ask for what cannot be, since this man is simply one of the shameless people who must exist. He applies the same reasoning to the sly, the unfaithful and every other kind of wrongdoer, and the effect is to replace surprise with calm.

Do not hope for Plato's perfect Republic, Marcus tells himself, for that is asking too much of a world made of ordinary people. Be content if even the smallest thing goes well, and do not regard such an outcome as unimportant. A ruler who had the power to try for great reforms is here teaching himself to value small improvements, and the lesson is a wise one for any leader.

As emperor, Marcus was also the chief priest of Rome, and he carried out the old ceremonies and sacrifices of the state with great care. In the notebook he often speaks of the gods and of a providence that rules the world, but he never argues about what exactly they are. Perhaps that is why his thoughts about the divine have been welcome to people of many religions, and to people of none.

Marcus likes to walk in imagination through the court of Augustus, the first emperor, and to count the people who were there, from his wife and daughter to his friends, his doctors and his priests. All of them, he notes, are dead, and the whole glittering court has vanished from the earth. A crowd that seemed so important and so permanent has passed away like a feast that is over, and the reader is left to draw the lesson for his own day.

It would be easy to expect a book so full of death to be a gloomy one, but the mood of the notebook is rarely bitter. Marcus uses the thought of the end to make himself gentler with other people, more patient with small annoyances and more attentive to the day in front of him. He seems to have found that a person who accepts that he will die has more attention to give to living.

Marcus liked to picture himself looking down on the world from a great height, watching the armies, the farms, the weddings and the lawsuits as a great and endless procession. He urges himself to run along with the stars in his imagination and to think of the constant change of all things. Seen from this distance, the quarrels that seem so large up close shrink to their true size, and the mind is freed from much of its anxiety.

Marcus likes to remind himself how small the earth is, a mere point in the vast universe, and how small a corner of it any one person occupies. The same is true of fame, he adds, for even the most famous man is known only to a few of the people in that corner, and soon to none. The proportions are humbling, but they are also freeing, since much of what we fear to lose is really very small.

Whoever has seen the present, Marcus writes, has seen everything that has ever happened from the beginning of time and everything that will happen in the endless future, for all things are of one kind and one form. The claim sounds exaggerated, but he means that human life repeats the same patterns, of hope and fear, love and quarrel, ambition and loss. A person who understands them in one place can recognise them anywhere, and finds that nothing is truly new.

Marcus says that everything is familiar, short-lived and mean in substance, and that all things now are just as they were in the days of those whom we have buried. The same dramas are performed again and again, with a new cast in each age and the same scenes of ambition, fear and farewell. It is a sobering view, and yet it makes life seem lighter, since there is no need to be shocked by what has happened so many times before.

Wipe out your imagination, Marcus tells himself, check your impulses, put out your desires and keep your ruling mind in your own power. The four commands read like the orders of a ship's captain in a storm, and in a way they are, for he is trying to steer his mind through rough water. They are also remarkably practical, since each one deals with a different way in which a person can lose control.

Marcus says that a person is composed of three things: a small body, a little breath and an intelligence. The first two are ours only in the sense that we must care for them, he explains, but the third, the mind, is properly our own. It follows that if we detach ourselves from what other people do and say, we can live out our lives free from compulsion, since the mind is the one possession that no one else can seize.

With a flash of sharp humour, Marcus says that a spider is proud when it catches a fly, and a man is proud when he catches a hare, a small fish, a wild boar or a bear. Another man, he adds, is proud when he captures a tribe, and the Sarmatians are the example he gives. They are all a kind of hunter, he suggests, and if their principles are examined they are not so different from robbers.

Marcus offers a list of images that must have felt close to home for an emperor, including a bone thrown to little dogs, a crumb of bread tossed into a fish pond and ants toiling under their loads. He adds frightened mice running to and fro, and puppets jerked about by their strings. These are the things, he says, that human beings fight and fuss over, and the pictures are comic, but the point is serious, which is that our busy activity is often much smaller than we imagine.

Marcus ends his comparison with a rule that has been quoted ever since, which is that every person is worth just as much as the things about which he busies himself. A man who spends his days on trifles becomes a trifling man, he suggests, and one who gives his attention to what is just and good becomes a person of weight. The measure is a hard one to face, and it is meant to be, because it asks us what we have really been caring about.

Marcus compares the experiences of life with an afternoon at the public baths, where one sees oil, sweat, dirt and greasy water. Looked at without sentiment, he says, every part of life and every object in it can seem as unlovely as that. The comparison is meant to remove the shine from the things we crave, and it has the same purpose as his comments on food, wine and purple robes.

Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be, Marcus tells himself, but go and be one. The sentence is blunt and a little impatient, as though he were scolding himself for spending too long on theory. For him, as for the other Stoics, philosophy was meant to be lived in the street, in the council chamber and in the camp, and not only discussed in the lecture room.

Live as if you were on a mountain, Marcus says, for it makes no difference whether a person lives here or there, so long as he lives everywhere as a citizen of the world. A man on a mountain is not troubled by the noise of the city, and a man at peace within is not troubled by the noise of the court. He adds that people should be allowed to see in him a real human being who lives according to nature.

Doctors always keep their instruments and their knives ready for sudden emergencies, Marcus observes, and a person should keep his principles just as ready for the understanding of things divine and human. The point is that wisdom is no use if it must be looked up in a book while the crisis is happening. It has to be learned so well that the hand reaches for it by itself, as a surgeon's hand reaches for the right tool.

It is a human being's proper work, Marcus says, and his proper delight, to be kind to his fellow human beings, to look down on the movements of the senses and to judge first appearances rightly. He should also study the nature of the universe and everything that happens in it. A list of four duties may seem a modest summary of a human life, but each of them is difficult, and together they make a program that a person could follow for a lifetime.

Marcus often tests a planned action with a few simple questions, such as whether it is really necessary and whether it serves the people around him. If the answer is no, he tells himself, he should leave it undone, since much of what we say and do is empty. The habit sounds modest, but a ruler who applied it to every order and every law would have governed very well indeed.

Death and life, honour and dishonour, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, Marcus says, all of these happen equally to good people and to bad ones, and being neither noble nor shameful in themselves, they are neither good nor evil. What makes a life good must therefore be something else, and the Stoic answer is character, which no one can hand out or take away. It is a hard teaching for someone who has a palace, and Marcus keeps repeating it for exactly that reason.

In the tenth book Marcus addresses his own soul and asks whether it will ever be good, simple, whole and plain to see, more visible than the body that surrounds it. Will it ever have a loving and contented nature, he asks, and be so full that it wants nothing more and longs for no pleasure of any kind? The questions are not rhetorical, and they show a man who still felt himself to be a beginner.

Marcus recalls an old line of poetry, which says that the wind scatters some leaves on the ground while the forest puts out new ones in spring, and that human generations are just like that. Your children are leaves, he says, and so are those who praise you or curse you, and so are those who will remember you after you are gone. The thought is melancholy, but he uses it to ask why people avoid and pursue things as though they would last for ever.

Do not disturb yourself by thinking about the future, Marcus tells himself, for you will come to it, if you must, bringing with you the same reason that you now use for the things of the present. Most of our fears are borrowed from tomorrow, and the Stoic cure is to remember that the person who will meet tomorrow is the same one who is sitting here now, with the same tools. It is good advice for any anxious person, and perhaps especially for an emperor who had so many reasons to worry.

Enter into every speaker's ruling mind, Marcus tells himself, and allow every other person to enter into yours. It is an old Stoic way of saying that we should listen with our whole attention, trying to grasp what a person really means and not merely the words that he uses. A ruler who practised it would be a better judge of people and cases, and Marcus clearly hoped to be one.

Marcus lists several thoughts to calm himself when other people provoke him, and one is to remember how much more harm anger and distress do than the things that cause them. He adds that those who do wrong usually do it unwillingly, since in the Stoic view no one chooses evil knowingly, and that soon both he and the offender will be dead. It is not a complete theory of anger, but it is a practical toolkit, and it shows how hard he worked at a temper that must often have been tested.

Kindness is invincible, Marcus writes, provided that it is sincere and not a smirk or a part played for effect. What could the most violent man do to you, he asks, if you kept up a gentle manner toward him and, when the chance arose, calmly tried to set him right? The idea is bold, and it does not promise that a kind answer will always work, but it shows how seriously he took the power of a patient and genuine goodwill.

When another person's behaviour makes you angry, Marcus tells himself, remember that you yourself have done many things wrong, and that you are in some ways just the same as he is. You cannot even be certain that he is wrong, he adds, since many actions are done for reasons that are hidden from us, and a person must learn a great deal before he can judge another's act. It is an uncomfortable but useful way to take the heat out of a quarrel.

Gentleness and mildness are more human than anger, Marcus argues, and so they are also more manly, for strength, nerve and courage belong to the person who is calm and not to the one who is angry and discontented. To a Roman soldier's ears this was a bold claim, and it overturned the usual idea of toughness. In his view, a man who is in a rage is not strong but is being pushed about by his own feelings.

If you have the chance to correct a person who has gone wrong, Marcus says, do it tenderly and with real affection, not as a schoolmaster would and not to impress the bystanders. Say that you are not hurt, and that he is the one who is hurting himself, and say it as though you meant it. It is a delicate art, and Marcus knew how rarely it is done well.

Marcus lists the special powers of the thinking soul, which sees itself, examines itself and makes of itself whatever it wishes. It also reaps its own harvest, he says, whereas the fruits of plants and the creatures of the field are gathered by others. The point is that a human being, alone among living things, can be his own gardener, and this is both an honour and a responsibility.

Marcus reflects that tragedies were first brought onto the stage to remind people of the things that happen in life, and to show that such things are natural. If we are pleased by what we see in a theatre, he says, we ought not to be troubled by the same events on the larger stage of the world. Even the heroes who cry out in grief on the stage bear their troubles, and we can learn to bear ours.

If anyone can convince me and show me that I do not think or act rightly, Marcus says, I will gladly change, for I am searching for the truth, which has never harmed anybody. What does harm people, he adds, is to persist in their self-deception and ignorance, and to refuse every correction. It is a fine statement of intellectual honesty, and it is all the more admirable coming from a man who held absolute power and was seldom contradicted.

When anyone does you a wrong, Marcus advises, think at once about what that person believed to be good and what to be bad. Once you have seen this, you will pity him, and you will be neither surprised nor angry, since he is acting on a mistaken picture of the world. The method does not excuse the wrong, but it replaces rage with understanding, and understanding is much easier to carry.

Marcus never claims to have mastered anger, and the very length of his lists of reminders suggests how often he needed them. The notebook is full of advice for staying calm, which is exactly what we might expect from a man who felt tempted to lose his temper. That is the kind of honesty that makes the book trustworthy, since it shows a student at work and not a master on a stage.

Epictetus, whom Marcus read with such attention, taught that human life is like a play in which each person has been given a part by the author. If the part is short, play it briefly, and if it is long, play it at length, and if the author wants you to play a beggar, a ruler or a cripple, play that well. For Marcus, whose part was the most public in the world, the lesson was a useful anchor.

The part that fate gave Marcus was the largest in the Roman world, and he seems to have known how easy it would be to be swallowed up by it. He warns himself not to become a Caesar, not to be dyed with that dye, and not to start acting as a ruler instead of being a man. The notebook is, in a way, a daily rehearsal for staying himself inside a costume that was very heavy to wear.

Everything that you hope to reach by a long and roundabout road, Marcus writes, you can have at this moment, if only you do not refuse it to yourself. You need only leave the past behind, trust the future to the course of events, and direct the present toward what is just and dutiful. For a person who had learned how little control anyone has over what comes next, it is a calming rule, and it directs attention to the only time in which a person can act.

Marcus confesses that he has often wondered how it is that every person loves himself more than anyone else, and yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinions of others. If a god or a wise teacher stood beside us and ordered us to speak no thought aloud that we had not already formed, he adds, we could not bear it for a single day. The remark is a sharp reminder to look to our own judgment first, and it applies as much to the age of social media as to the age of Rome.

If it is not right, do not do it, Marcus says, and if it is not true, do not say it. The rule is so short that it can be carried in the head all day, and it is hard to find a situation in which it does not apply. For a man who was surrounded by flatterers and had many reasons to say what pleased others, it was a protection as much as a rule.

Stop wandering about, Marcus tells himself, since you are not likely to read your own notes again, and hurry toward the end that is in front of you. Throw away idle hopes, he says, and come to your own help while you can, if you care at all about yourself. It is a surprising line to find in a notebook, because it admits that the writing is useful only if it leads to action.

Return to your senses and call yourself back, Marcus tells himself, and when you have woken from sleep and seen that it was only dreams that troubled you, look at the things around you with the same waking eyes. It is a startling image, because it suggests that a great deal of what alarms us has the same flimsy quality as a bad dream. The cure for both, he says, is simply to wake up properly and to look again at what is really there.

Epictetus liked to say that everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. If a brother treats you unfairly, he explained, do not take hold of the matter by the handle of his injustice, for it cannot be carried that way. Take hold of it instead by the other handle, which is that he is your brother and was raised beside you, a habit that Marcus absorbed and that runs through his notebook.

Roman writers say that Marcus took his duties as a judge very seriously, hearing cases patiently and giving them careful attention, even when the hours were long. They also credit him with laws that protected orphans, slaves who wished to be freed, and others who had little power. It is hard to know how much of this is flattery, but it fits the character that he sets out in his own notebook.

The calm that Marcus seeks is not the quiet of a man with no worries, for he had an empire to rule, a war to fight, a family to lose and a body that often hurt. It is the calm of someone who has practised carrying heavy things, and who has learned which parts of the load are really his. The notebook suggests that such calm is not a gift but a skill, and that skill can be learned a little at a time.

You may leave life this very moment, Marcus reminds himself, and let that fact decide what you do, what you say and what you think. He returns to the idea so often that it becomes almost a refrain, and it is meant not to frighten but to focus. A person who knows that time is short, he believes, has little patience left for pettiness, and no reason to postpone kindness.

In the last book Marcus speaks to himself as a citizen of the great city of the world, and he asks what it matters whether he has lived in it for five years or three. What is according to law is equal for everyone, he says, so there is nothing terrible in leaving. It is a comforting argument, because it takes away the sting of comparing a long life with a short one.

In the last book Marcus compares life to a play in which the actor is dismissed from the stage by the very director who hired him. I have not finished the five acts, the actor complains, but only three of them, and Marcus answers that in life three acts are the whole drama, for it is nature that decides when a play is complete. The man who leaves, he adds, may depart with a good grace, since the one who lets him go is not unkind.

Why should it be a hardship to be sent away from the city, Marcus asks, when the one who sends us is not a tyrant or an unjust judge but nature, the same power that brought us in? The question changes the whole picture of death, since it replaces a cruel enemy with an old friend. He does not say that it is always easy to see it this way, only that it is reasonable.

The notebook's last lines are an invitation to depart cheerfully, because the one who releases you, Marcus says, is also cheerful. After a book full of reminders about duty and effort, the final note is one of release and peace. Whether or not Marcus knew what would become of these pages, the ending feels like a fitting farewell to the whole work.

Epictetus advised his students never to say of anything that they had lost it, but only that they had given it back, and this includes a child and one's own life. Marcus, who lost several children, would have known what a hard teaching it was. His own reminders about leaving as one who returns a loan, with thanks and without bitterness, are written in the same spirit.

If it is no evil for each thing in the world to be continually changed into another, Marcus asks, why should a person fear the change and breaking up of everything, including himself? It happens according to nature, he says, and nothing that is according to nature can be evil. The argument is logical rather than comforting, but many readers find that it works on them in a way that gentle words do not.

Epictetus taught that death is nothing terrible, since if it were, it would have seemed so to Socrates, who met his own with great calm. The terror lies in the opinion that death is terrible, he said, and so it is our opinion that we must change. Marcus knew the argument well, and he repeats it in his own way when he tells himself that fear belongs to the judgment and not to the event.

The twelfth book ends with that farewell, and the notebook stops without a summary, a signature or a word of explanation. We cannot tell whether Marcus planned to write more, or whether this was simply the place where the surviving pages came to an end. Either way, the final note leaves the reader with the same quiet invitation to carry on and to do the day's work well.

Marcus says that a person lives with the gods when he constantly shows them a soul that is satisfied with what is given to it and does everything that the divine spirit within him wishes. He ties the idea of a good death to the idea of a good life, and suggests that anyone who lives in this way has already made his peace. For readers who do not share his religion, the same thought can be read as a picture of inner harmony.

In 169 Marcus left Rome for the northern frontier, and from then on he spent most of his remaining years there, with only a few returns to the capital. Roman armies fought the Marcomanni, the Quadi and the Sarmatians along the Danube, and the wars were long, hard and costly. He had never wished to be a general, but he did what duty required, and the notebook is the record of the thoughts that kept him steady.

A famous story tells how a sudden storm saved a thirsty and trapped Roman army around the year 172, soaking the soldiers while lightning scattered their enemies. Pagan writers credited different gods or even an Egyptian magician, while Christian writers credited the prayers of Christian soldiers, and a figure of a rain god appears on Marcus's column. Historians disagree about how much of it is true, and, so far as we can tell, the notebook does not mention it.

In 175 Avidius Cassius, a gifted general who commanded the eastern provinces, declared himself emperor, perhaps after hearing a false rumour that Marcus had died. Marcus, who was far away on the Danube, made peace with the northern tribes and prepared to march east. Before he could arrive, Cassius's own officers killed him, and the revolt fell apart after about three months.

Roman writers report that Marcus was unusually merciful after the revolt, pardoning many who had supported the rebel and showing kindness to his family. One writer even says that he burned the letters found among Cassius's papers without reading them, so that he would not learn who had been disloyal. The stories may be polished by admirers, but they fit the man who wrote that the best revenge is not to become like the wrongdoer.

In 175 Marcus lost his wife Faustina, who had travelled with him on campaign and died at a small place in Cappadocia, far from Rome. He mourned her publicly and honoured her memory, and the little town was renamed Faustinopolis in her honour. Ancient writers disagree about her character, but Marcus himself gave thanks to the gods in his notebook for a wife who was loving and unpretentious.

Wars cost money, and ancient writers say that Marcus raised it by holding a great sale in the Forum of Trajan, where he sold gold cups, silk robes, jewels and statues from the imperial palace. He did this, they say, rather than add new taxes to a population already suffering from plague. The story may be exaggerated in its details, but it matches the sense of duty and simplicity that the notebook shows.

In 177 Marcus made his teenage son Commodus joint emperor, which secured the succession but tied the empire's future to a young man who was vain and unready. The emperors before Marcus had each chosen the best man available and adopted him, but this time the throne passed from father to son, and many historians believe it was a mistake. It is one of the few decisions in his life that Marcus's admirers find hard to defend.

The famous doctor Galen, who served the imperial household, wrote that Marcus often suffered from pain in the stomach and chest, and that he took a well-known medicine called theriac to ease it. Whatever his health, the emperor did not spare himself, and his notebook gives the impression of a man who worked on while tired or in discomfort. It adds a human detail to the picture of a ruler who is so often described as a marble statue.

Marcus died in March of 180 while still on campaign near the Danube, and the ancient writers disagree about whether the place was Vindobona, which is today's Vienna, or Sirmium. He was fifty-eight years old, and illness is said to have been the cause, though the details are uncertain. His son Commodus, who had been named joint emperor a few years earlier, took the throne, and many historians regard his father's death as the end of a long period of relative stability.

After his death Rome raised a tall column carved with scenes of the northern wars, which still stands in the city today. A bronze statue of Marcus on horseback, with one hand held out in a gesture of calm, also survives, perhaps because the people of the Middle Ages mistook it for Constantine, the first Christian emperor. The calm of that raised hand suits the man who wrote the notebook, and many visitors to Rome still stop to look at it.

After Marcus died in 180, the little notebook was somehow kept, although it had never been meant for anyone's eyes but his own. We do not know who found it, who decided that it was worth saving, or how it came to be copied, and the early record is almost silent. That it survived at all, through plague, war and the slow collapse of the western empire, seems a small miracle.

For many centuries the notebook survived only in copies made by hand by Greek scribes, and only a handful of writers mention it. Around the year 900 a Greek churchman named Arethas owned a copy and wrote about it, and his note is an important early record of the book. Only a few manuscripts survive today, which means that the book had a narrow escape.

In 1559 the first printed edition appeared in Zurich, prepared by the German scholar Wilhelm Xylander, who also provided a Latin translation. He had worked from a manuscript that has since been lost, so his book is a precious witness. From then on, the Meditations could travel through Europe in print, and its readers were no longer limited to those who could reach a monastery library.

The first English translation was made by Meric Casaubon, a scholar of French descent, and it was published in London in 1634. Many others have followed, and the book has been translated into dozens of languages and is rarely out of print. Each translator has had to decide how to turn a private Greek jotting into plain English, and the many versions show how much room that leaves.

The Meditations is not an argument built step by step but a collection of notes, some of them only a line long and some a page, set down in no tidy order. Marcus repeats himself on purpose, since a person who wants to change a habit of mind has to rehearse the same truths again and again. It is best read slowly, a few passages at a time, in the way that it was written.

It would be wrong to picture Marcus as a flawless sage, for he was a Roman emperor who commanded armies, accepted the harsh realities of his age and made decisions that people still debate. What the notebook shows is a person who knows his own weaknesses, such as anger, tiredness and discouragement, and who writes in order to correct them. That is much of its appeal, since it is the work of someone who is trying and not someone who has arrived.

Kings, soldiers, poets and ordinary readers have all turned to the notebook in hard times. Frederick the Great of Prussia is said to have admired Marcus greatly, and in the nineteenth century the poet and critic Matthew Arnold wrote about him with deep affection. Today the book is read in offices, hospitals, gyms and kitchens, by people who have never given a thought to the Roman Empire.

Soldiers, leaders, students and ordinary readers have all found something in the Meditations, partly because its advice is brief and honest and partly because it speaks about problems that never go away. Anger, fear, tiredness, disappointment and the awareness of death were as familiar in a Roman army camp as they are in a modern office. It is also a rare example of a very powerful person using his private writing to hold himself to account.

Some readers follow the example of Marcus and keep a notebook of their own, in which they write short reminders about what they can control and what they cannot. The habit asks very little, perhaps a few honest lines each morning or evening, but it turns philosophy from an idea into a daily practice. There is no promise that it will remove trouble, only the hope that it will make us a little steadier in meeting it.

In the end, the Meditations offers no cure for the hardships of life, only a few steady ideas, which are that we should master our thoughts, do our duty, be kind to others and accept what we cannot change. Marcus did not write them for us, but for himself, and he kept writing them down because he knew how easily they slip away. Each morning, he seems to say, a person may begin again, and the lamp that he trimmed in his tent on the frontier still gives light to anyone who opens his book.
